\title{Dyadic divisor products and rectangular multiplication tables}
\author{Tseng}
\date{}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
For every fixed integer $k\ge1$, we determine the order of magnitude of
$H^{(k+1)}(x,\mathbf y,2\mathbf y)$, the number of integers $n\le x$
divisible by a product $d_1\cdots d_k$ with $y_i<d_i\le2y_i$.
The estimate is uniform for $3\le y_1\le\cdots\le y_k$ and
$x\ge2^k y_1\cdots y_k y_k$. It yields a uniform formula for the
number of distinct products in every rectangular multiplication table
with real ordered side lengths $1\le N_1\le\cdots\le N_{k+1}$.
The formula covers coincident cutoffs, bounded sides, and rectangles
in which several saddle constraints are active. Its main exponential
term comes from an ordered saddle; the remaining factors measure
count windows, divisor overlap, and a terminal bridge. The overlap
factors involve fractional moments of conditional Ornstein--Uhlenbeck
survival probabilities. We also establish a locally $C^{1,1}$
positive-order persistence spectrum, a strict annealing gap, and a full
large-deviation principle for the scalar conditional survival cost.
\end{abstract}
\tableofcontents
\clearpage

\section{Introduction}
\label{paper:introduction}

The size of a multiplication table measures how much distinct integer
factorizations overlap. In a rectangular table, the different side
lengths impose constraints at different prime scales. Our aim is to
retain all of these constraints and obtain an estimate uniform in the
shape of the rectangle, for every fixed number of factors.

For an ordered vector of side lengths, put
\[
 A_{k+1}(\mathbf N)
 =\#\{n_1\cdots n_{k+1}:n_i\in\mathbb N,\ n_i\le N_i\}.
\]
The dyadic divisor count associated with this problem is
\[
 H^{(k+1)}(x,\mathbf y,2\mathbf y)
 =\#\{n\le x:\exists d_1,\ldots,d_k\in\mathbb N,
       \ y_i<d_i\le2y_i,\ d_1\cdots d_k\mid n\}.
\]
We determine its order of magnitude uniformly throughout
\[
 3\le y_1\le\cdots\le y_k,
 \qquad x\ge2^k(y_1\cdots y_k)y_k,
\]
for every fixed $k$. The resulting profile also determines
$A_{k+1}(\mathbf N)$ uniformly for every real ordered vector
$1\le N_1\le\cdots\le N_{k+1}$. The conclusions are stated in
Theorems~\ref{new:main} and \ref{table:main}. All comparison constants
depend only on $k$; no separation between adjacent cutoffs or bounds
on their ratios are imposed.

\subsection{Earlier results and the rectangular obstruction}

The multiplication-table problem asks for the number of distinct
integers among the products $ab$, with $1\le a,b\le N$. Erd\H{o}s
\cite{Erdos1955} proved that this number is $o(N^2)$. Thus the
multiplicity of integer factorizations changes the scale of the
problem, even though there are $N^2$ ordered pairs. Ford
\cite[Corollary~3]{FordDivisors2008} determined its order of magnitude:
\[
 \#\{ab:1\le a,b\le N\}
 \asymp \frac{N^2}{(\log N)^\delta(\log\log N)^{3/2}},
 \qquad
 \delta=1-\frac{1+\log\log2}{\log2}.
\]
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Erdos1960} had earlier established
$N^2(\log N)^{-\delta+o(1)}$ as the scale of the square table.
Tenenbaum \cite{Tenenbaum1984} developed estimates for the more general
count $H^{(2)}(x,y,z)$ of integers with a divisor in $(y,z]$.
Ford's interval theorem \cite[Corollary~2]{FordDivisors2008} gives
\[
 H^{(2)}(x,y,2y)\asymp
 \frac{x}{(\log y)^\delta(\log\log y)^{3/2}}
 \qquad(3\le y\le\sqrt{x}).
\]
His separate treatment of the dyadic case \cite{FordDyadic2008}
exposes the divisor-clustering and order-statistics estimates used in
the later generalizations. The small exponent $\delta$ reflects the balance
between the scarcity of integers with sufficiently many prime factors
and the overlap among their divisors.

For higher-dimensional balanced tables, Koukoulopoulos
\cite[Corollary~1]{KoukLocal} established, for every fixed $k\ge2$,
\[
 A_{k+1}(N,\ldots,N)
 \asymp_k
 \frac{N^{k+1}}{(\log N)^{Q(k/\log(k+1))}
                    (\log\log N)^{3/2}},
 \qquad Q(u)=u\log u-u+1,
\]
for $N\ge3$. His subsequent work \cite{Kouk} treats rectangular
tables through a comparison with dyadic divisor counts
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{Kouk}. In conjunction with Ford's dyadic estimate,
this comparison also gives all two-dimensional rectangles with sides
at least $3$. For $2\le k\le5$, Theorem~1.3 of \cite{Kouk} gives
a uniform estimate for arbitrary ordered cutoffs and hence tables
with three through six factors. For $k\ge6$, Theorem~1.4 gives a
matching estimate when $\log y_k\le(\log y_1)^{1+\varepsilon_k}$
for a suitable $\varepsilon_k>0$. Theorem~1.5 gives an upper bound
for every fixed $k\ge2$, and a matching lower bound under a restriction
on the saddle parameter.\footnote{In the
notation of \cite{Kouk}, let $h_i=k-i+2$ and
$\ell_i=\log(3\log y_i/\log y_{i-1})$, with $y_0=3$. The
parameter $\alpha$ is determined by
$\sum_i h_i^\alpha(\log h_i)\ell_i=\sum_i(h_i-1)\ell_i$.
For fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the matching lower bound in Theorem~1.5
requires $\alpha\ge1+\varepsilon-
(\log(k+1))^{-1}\log(((k+1)\log(k+1)-2\log2)/(k-1))$; its
constants may depend on $k$ and $\varepsilon$.}
His analysis of the additional constraints
\cite[Section~2.2, Lemma~2.3 and Remark~2.4]{Kouk} explains why
the single-parameter expression can overestimate some
higher-dimensional rectangles. The remaining unrestricted dimensions
are also discussed in \cite[Chapter~6, pp.~87--88]{KoukThesis2010}.
The ordered saddle below retains distinct constraints on successive
prime ranges.

Related work makes the subset-sum structure of divisor overlap
particularly transparent. Eberhard, Ford and Green
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{EberhardFordGreen2016} proved
that the probability that a uniformly random permutation in $S_n$
has an invariant $j$-element set is
$\asymp j^{-\delta}(1+\log j)^{-3/2}$, uniformly for
$1\le j\le n/2$. Ford, Green and Koukoulopoulos
\cite{FordGreenKoukoulopoulos2023} developed higher-dimensional
optimization methods for equal subset sums and the concentration of
divisors. More recently, Green and Sawhney
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{GreenSawhney2026} proved an asymptotic for the
limiting invariant-set probability, with a smooth positive periodic
factor in $\log_2 j$. They conjecture that this factor is nonconstant.
Sawhney's report of joint work with Green
\cite{SawhneyGreenAnnouncement2025} announces an integer square-table
asymptotic with a periodic amplitude; the permutation preprint
describes the integer treatment as forthcoming. These refinements
are distinct from the uniform comparison estimates sought here.
In a different regime, Sabuncu and T\'afula
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{SabuncuTafula2026} determine the asymptotic leading
coefficient of the eventual polynomial in the dimension for tables
with a common side length. Their result applies as the side length
tends to infinity and the dimension is sufficiently large in terms
of that side length. Section~\ref{sec:open-problems} discusses the
extension to variable-dimensional rectangles.

\subsection{Divisor overlap and the proof architecture}
\label{intro:architecture}

The arithmetic starting point is Koukoulopoulos's reduction
\cite[Theorem~1.7]{Kouk} to a harmonic sum of volumes of divisor-box
unions. A prime in $(y_{i-1},y_i]$ can be used in divisor coordinate
$i$ or any later coordinate, or left unused. An assignment of all
primes to these categories is a routing word. Its divisor vector,
on the logarithmic scale, determines a box of fixed side length.
The volume of the union counts the space covered by these words,
with overlaps counted only once. Estimating that volume is the
geometric form of the original counting problem.

Two effects determine its size. The prime counts must be large enough
to provide sufficiently many routing words, but the words can cluster
if too many small primes accumulate before a coordinate's cutoff.
The saddle balances the cost of the counts against the available
volume. For rectangles, this balance has to respect the order of the
coordinates. Consecutive equal saddle coordinates form a plateau;
a strict drop between plateaux gives a separate count-window cost.
Within a plateau, comparisons between words give path constraints
whose endpoint reserves are calculated from a finite list of legal
contexts. The ordered saddle and these endpoint costs keep track of
the constraints that a single saddle parameter can lose.

The resulting profile has four parts. The saddle gives the main
exponential term. Strict drops give count-window factors. The path
constraints within each plateau give binary persistence factors.
A final ordinary bridge and its exact count atom give the terminal
factor. Section~\ref{profile:definition} defines each part and combines
them in \eqref{profile:raw}. In dimension one there are no binary
factors: the saddle and the ordinary factor recover Ford's dyadic
estimate. The balanced case is recovered in
Section~\ref{assembly:special-cases}.
Two worked profiles in Section~\ref{profile:examples} show how the
endpoint and suffix rules change the polynomial factors, including a
family with a strict saddle separation.

The binary factors require a conditional probability. Prime positions
are common to all routing words, whereas their labels vary from word
to word. We therefore fix the positions, sum the admissible label mass,
take its fractional power, and only then average over positions.
Averaging the labels and positions together at the outset would lose
the dependence relevant to divisor overlap. This distinction leads
to the exponent $\chi(\eta,\rho)$, defined by fractional moments of
conditional Ornstein--Uhlenbeck survival. The use of fractional moments
builds on \cite[Section~1]{KoukLocal}; the separation of the common
positions from the private labels is what determines the exponent
needed here. Section~\ref{profile:heuristic} explains how a count model
predicts the saddle cost, where that prediction loses projected volume,
and why a conditional bridge produces the endpoint factor with exponent
$2\chi$.

The lower and upper bounds use this profile in different ways.
For the lower bound, we construct a measure on complete count types,
including the exact terminal count, and then impose the path constraints
conditional on each type. Spatial clocks are independent at this stage.
Transport of the label measure places the surviving words at compatible
endpoints; a fractional bound for their intersections converts their
mass into a lower bound for the divisor-box volume. For the upper
bound, ordered covers successively restrict the available divisor
coordinates. Their estimates preserve the plateau powers and leave
one terminal count unread. Its atom and path constraint are integrated
jointly, producing the same ordinary factor as in the lower bound.

Here is the order of the argument. Section~\ref{paper:arithmetic-setup}
states the arithmetic theorems and the harmonic representation.
Section~\ref{profile:definition} defines the profile, and
Section~\ref{paper:geometry} proves the saddle and endpoint properties
on which it rests. Section~\ref{pr:section} develops conditional
survival estimates; Section~\ref{sec:bridges} transfers them to marked
bridges under exact conditioning. Sections~\ref{lower:chapter}--\ref{lower:intersections}
construct the count measure, transport it, and prove the volume lower
bound. The deterministic and arithmetic upper bounds culminate in
Section~\ref{sec:positive-core}. Harmonic stability in
Section~\ref{paper:assembly} then extends both estimates to coincident
cutoffs, and Section~\ref{table:section} proves the rectangular theorem,
including bounded sides.

The persistence theory also has consequences beyond the arithmetic
estimate. Mallein and Mi{\l}o\'s \cite{MalleinMilos2018} established
almost-sure Brownian and Ornstein--Uhlenbeck survival exponents above
an independent random wall. For the fractional-moment exponent used
here, Section~\ref{pr:section} proves uniform finite-time comparisons,
a positive-order spectrum with local $C^{1,1}$ regularity, and a strict
annealing gap. Appendix~\ref{fp:app:ldp} gives the scalar
large-deviation theory and identifies the almost-sure exponent with
the derivative at order zero. That appendix is independent of the
arithmetic assembly.

The remaining appendices supply the detailed endpoint geometry,
count and intersection estimates, prime discretization, and numerical
choices of constants. Each begins with the role of its estimates in
the main proof. Numbering in citations to \cite{Kouk} refers throughout
to arXiv:1102.3236v3; numbering for \cite{KoukLocal} refers to the
author version linked in the bibliography. Where the published and
revised versions of \cite{FordDyadic2008} differ, the version used is
specified at the citation.

\subsection{Notation}

All logarithms are natural, and $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$. The
dimension $k$ is fixed. We write $f\ll_k g$ if $f\le C_k g$ for a
constant depending only on $k$, and $f\asymp_k g$ if both inequalities
hold. Empty products equal $1$, and a minimum over an empty list is
$+\infty$. We put $(u)_+=\max(u,0)$ and use Lebesgue measure for
volumes. Probability laws and conditioning fields are specified where
they enter the proof. Within a section, or a numbered appendix
subsection, an equation reference may omit its prefix.

\section{Main results and the harmonic representation}
\label{paper:arithmetic-setup}
We first state the two arithmetic conclusions. Their common profile is
specified by the finite saddle and endpoint rules in
Section~\ref{profile:definition}; the universal scalar exponent used
there is defined probabilistically and has effective finite-time
approximations. The proofs estimate one harmonic volume sum, which is
introduced after the theorem statements.

For the dyadic count, let
\[
 H^{(k+1)}(x,\mathbf y,2\mathbf y)
 =\#\{n\in\mathbb N:n\le x,\ \exists d_1,\ldots,d_k,
       \ y_i<d_i\le2y_i,\ d_1\cdots d_k\mid n\}.
\]
Put $H=k+1$, $y_0=3$ and
\[
 L_i=\log\frac{\log y_i}{\log y_{i-1}}\ge0,
 \qquad \ell_i=L_i+\log3.
\]
The lengths $L_i$ measure the widths of the successive prime ranges
on the $\log\log$ scale. A coincident pair of cutoffs gives a zero
length. To state a single formula covering this boundary, let
$\Lambda_k$ be the fixed constant specified in
Appendix~\ref{supp:explicit-fixed-lift-rule}.
For $L_i^*=\max(L_i,\Lambda_k)$ use the finite rules in
Section~\ref{profile:definition} and the scalar inverse evaluator in
Appendix~\ref{supp:ordered-saddle-scalar-elimination} to compute
$\Psi_k(L^*)$. Define
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\ F_k^{\rm dyad}(\mathbf y)
          =\Phi_k(\ell)=\Psi_k(L^*)\ }.
 \label{profile:final}
\end{equation}
The fixed lift changes the harmonic sum by a factor depending only
on the dimension; this is proved in Section~\ref{paper:assembly}.
It is used to evaluate the profile, while the divisor count retains
the given cutoffs and its stated range of $x$. The scalar recursion in
Appendix~\ref{supp:ordered-saddle-scalar-elimination} also covers
saddle coordinates that coincide.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform dyadic formula]\label{new:main}
For each fixed $k\ge1$ there are positive constants $c_k,C_k$ such that
for every $3\le y_1\le\cdots\le y_k$ and every
$x\ge2^k(y_1\cdots y_k)y_k$,
\[
 c_k F_k^{\rm dyad}(\mathbf y)
 \le\frac{H^{(k+1)}(x,\mathbf y,2\mathbf y)}x
 \le C_k F_k^{\rm dyad}(\mathbf y).
\]
The estimate includes equal adjacent cutoffs.
\end{theorem}

For real ordered side lengths $1\le N_1\le\cdots\le N_{k+1}$, let
\[
 A_{k+1}(\mathbf N)
 =\#\{n_1\cdots n_{k+1}:n_i\in\mathbb N,\ n_i\le N_i\}.
\]
Each distinct product is counted once.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform multiplication-table formula]
\label{table:main}
For each fixed integer $k\ge1$, uniformly for all real
$1\le N_1\le\cdots\le N_{k+1}$,
\[
 A_{k+1}(\mathbf N)
 \asymp_k\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k+1}N_i\right)
             \Phi_k\bigl(\ell(\mathbf Y)\bigr),
 \qquad Y_i=\max\{3,N_i/2\}.
\]
Equivalently, with the same dimension-dependent lift as in the dyadic
theorem, the profile here is
\[
 \Phi_k\bigl(\ell(\mathbf Y)\bigr)
 =\Psi_k\left(
     \left(\max\left\{
       \log\frac{\log Y_i}{\log Y_{i-1}},\Lambda_k
     \right\}\right)_{i=1}^k\right),\qquad Y_0=3.
\]
\end{theorem}

The normalization by the product of the side lengths makes the table
formula comparable to the density in Theorem~\ref{new:main}. The largest
side enters this product but does not add a cutoff to the profile.
Section~\ref{table:section} proves the transfer and treats the bounded
sides by a comparison with tables of lower dimension.

\subsection{Divisor boxes and the harmonic sum}

The arithmetic reduction replaces existence of a divisor product by
the volume covered by its possible logarithmic divisor vectors.
Let $\mathcal A_k(\mathbf y)$ consist of squarefree
pairwise coprime tuples $\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$, whose primes in
$a_1$ are at most $y_1$ and whose primes in $a_i$ for $i>1$ lie in
$(y_{i-1},y_i]$. Empty selections are allowed, and $2,3$ are in the
first prime range. Set
\begin{align}
 \mathcal L^{(k+1)}(\mathbf a)
 &=\bigcup_{\substack{d_1,\ldots,d_k\in\mathbb N\\
        d_1\cdots d_j\mid a_1\cdots a_j\ (1\le j\le k)}}
       \prod_{j=1}^k[\log(d_j/2),\log d_j),
       \label{paper:divisor-boxes}\\
 L^{(k+1)}(\mathbf a)&=\operatorname{vol}_k\mathcal L^{(k+1)}(\mathbf a),\notag\\
 K_k(\ell)&=e^{-\sum_i h_iL_i}
       \sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_k(\mathbf y)}
          \frac{L^{(k+1)}(\mathbf a)}{a_1\cdots a_k},
       \qquad h_i=k-i+2.\label{paper:K}
\end{align}
Each prime in group $i$ has $h_i$ possible labels: one for each eligible
divisor coordinate and one for nonuse. Thus the prefix divisibility
conditions in \eqref{paper:divisor-boxes} express precisely the ordered
routing rule. The reciprocal weights give the harmonic prime measure,
and the exponential factor in \eqref{paper:K} provides its normalization.
The empty tuple has unnormalized contribution $(\log2)^k$.

The arithmetic comparison of Koukoulopoulos
\cite[Theorem~1.7]{Kouk} states, with the harmless normalization above,
\begin{equation}
 H^{(k+1)}(x,\mathbf y,2\mathbf y)/x\asymp_k K_k(\ell)
 \qquad\bigl(x\ge2^k(y_1\cdots y_k)y_k\bigr).
 \label{main:admissible}
\end{equation}
The comparison is applied at the given cutoffs $\mathbf y$ and
with the stated range of $x$.

\begin{theorem}[Harmonic formula]\label{main:uniform}
With \eqref{new:lift}, $K_k(\ell)\asymp_k\Psi_k(L^*)$ on
$[\log3,\infty)^k$.
\end{theorem}
The lower bound is established in Section~\ref{lower:chapter},
the upper bound in Section~\ref{sec:positive-core}, and the passage to
all nonnegative block lengths in Section~\ref{paper:assembly}.

\subsection{Size truncation of the harmonic volume sum}
\label{artrunc:section}

The geometric covers used for the upper bound need an a priori bound
on the logarithmic width available to each coordinate. Such a bound
holds when the tuple is truncated in size, whereas the harmonic sum
in \eqref{paper:K} includes every squarefree tuple. The next lemma shows
that this truncation retains a fixed fraction of the weighted volume.
Its proof uses only the effect of inserting one prime, so it is available
before either sharp bound is proved.

Fix $H=k+1$ and $3\leq y_1\leq\cdots\leq y_k$. Write
$V(\mathbf a)=L^{(k+1)}(\mathbf a)$ and
\[
 S(\mathbf y)=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_k(\mathbf y)}
             \frac{V(\mathbf a)}{a_1\cdots a_k}.
\]
All prime sets here are finite; in particular all following rearrangements
are identities between finite nonnegative sums. Choose one absolute
constant $C_{\rm W}$ for the elementary weighted prime estimate
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{p\leq y}\frac{\log p}{p}\leq C_{\rm W}\log y
 \qquad(y\geq3).
 \label{artrunc:weighted-primes}
\end{equation}
For example the usual Chebyshev bound for $\sum_{p\leq y}\log p$ and
partial summation give this estimate; see
\cite[Theorem~9]{RosserSchoenfeld1962}. Put
\[
 \tau_k=2kH C_{\rm W}+1,
 \qquad
 S_{\rm tr}(\mathbf y)=
 \sum_{\substack{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_k(\mathbf y)\\
                         a_i\leq y_i^{\tau_k}\ (1\leq i\leq k)}}
                \frac{V(\mathbf a)}{a_1\cdots a_k}.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Uniform positive weighted truncation]
\label{artrunc:lemma}
Uniformly in the ordered cutoffs,
\begin{equation}
 S_{\rm tr}(\mathbf y)\leq S(\mathbf y)
                   \leq2 S_{\rm tr}(\mathbf y).
 \label{artrunc:comparison}
\end{equation}
The same comparison holds after multiplication by the exact normalizing
factor defining $K_k$. Every truncated tuple has, for each $i$,
\begin{equation}
 \log(a_1\cdots a_i)
       \leq\tau_k\sum_{g\leq i}\log y_g
       \leq k\tau_k\log y_i.
 \label{artrunc:prefix-size}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $p$ be a prime in original block $i$, and remove it from that
coordinate of a squarefree tuple. Inserting $p$ back permits at most
$k-i+2\leq H$ eligible routing labels, including the unused label.
For each label the new divisor-box union is a translate of the old
one. Therefore, if $p$ does not already divide the tuple,
\begin{equation}
 V(b_1,\ldots,pb_i,\ldots,b_k)\leq H V(\mathbf b).
 \label{artrunc:slot-growth}
\end{equation}
Using the squarefree identity $\log a_i=\sum_{p\mid a_i}\log p$ gives
the exact decomposition
\begin{align}
 \sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_k(\mathbf y)}
       \frac{V(\mathbf a)\log a_i}{a_1\cdots a_k}
 &=\sum_{p\text{ in block }i}\frac{\log p}{p}
       \sum_{\substack{\mathbf b\in\mathcal A_k(\mathbf y)\\p\nmid b_i}}
       \frac{V(b_1,\ldots,pb_i,\ldots,b_k)}{b_1\cdots b_k}
       \notag\\
 &\leq H S(\mathbf y)
                \sum_{p\text{ in block }i}\frac{\log p}{p}
 \leq H C_{\rm W}\log y_i\,S(\mathbf y).
 \label{artrunc:first-moment}
\end{align}
The prime blocks are disjoint, so removal and reinsertion in this
identity preserve every original prime-range restriction. In the
inequality we only enlarged the inner nonnegative sum.

For the bad set $a_i>y_i^{\tau_k}$, multiply its indicator by
$\log a_i/(\tau_k\log y_i)\geq1$ and use
\eqref{artrunc:first-moment}. A union bound over $i$ yields
\[
 S(\mathbf y)-S_{\rm tr}(\mathbf y)
 \leq\frac{kH C_{\rm W}}{\tau_k}S(\mathbf y)
 <\frac12S(\mathbf y).
\]
This proves \eqref{artrunc:comparison}. The common normalizing factor
does not change its ratio. Finally \eqref{artrunc:prefix-size} follows
from the individual size bounds and the ordering of the cutoffs.
\end{proof}

For the covers, \eqref{artrunc:prefix-size} supplies the required
baseline rectangle: every coordinate using only primes from the first
$i$ groups has logarithmic width at most $C_k\log y_i$. The contribution
of earlier groups to a later coordinate obeys the corresponding bound
at the last earlier cutoff. Here $C_k=k\tau_k$; its fixed powers are
absorbed into the cover constants and reserves. The lengths, saddle
coordinates, and plateaux remain those of the given vector.

The order of application is useful to keep explicit. We apply the
covers to the truncated squarefree sum, where the size bounds hold,
and then enlarge the positive sums to allow repeated primes and cell
approximations. Lemma~\ref{artrunc:lemma} transfers the resulting upper
bound to the full harmonic sum.


\section{The structural profile}
\label{profile:definition}

Throughout, $k\geq1$ is fixed, $H=k+1$, and $V_i=\sum_{g\leq i}L_g$,
with $V_0=0$. We define the profile for $L_i\geq1$; the fixed lift
in \eqref{profile:final} then extends it to $L_i\geq0$.

A fine routing word assigns each prime from range $i$ either to a
divisor coordinate $c\geq i$ or to the unused category. Its logarithmic
divisor vector is a sum of vectors $(\log p)e_c$, where $e_c$
is the $c$th coordinate vector. Different assignments
can produce overlapping boxes of side length $\log2$, so the problem
depends on the overlap of these ordered subset sums as well as on the
number of assignments.

In the Poisson model, the uncolored prime positions form a common
environment. We sum the conditional mass of admissible routing words
before raising it to a fractional power, and then average over this
environment. This order retains the dependence among the count types
and the path constraints.

The definitions below follow the four sources of cost described in
Section~\ref{intro:architecture}. The ordered saddle fixes the tilted
prime intensities and the plateaux. Endpoint costs then specify how
much reserve is available to each binary path comparison. Conditional
survival converts these reserves into persistence factors. Finally,
a terminal ordinary bridge supplies the root factor. All enumerations have size bounded in terms of the fixed dimension $k$.
The constants in the construction depend only on $k$.

The distinction between a group and a plateau is used throughout.
A group is a prescribed prime range and keeps its own spatial clock.
A plateau is a run of equal saddle coordinates and determines which
label comparisons share a fractional power. Several groups can
therefore belong to one plateau without being combined into one clock.

\subsection{The saddle and the prime ranges}
For a prime in group $i$, one choice uses coordinate $i$ and the
remaining choices continue to later coordinates or to nonuse.
If the current fractional power is $s_i$, a tail with effective
weight $Z_{i+1}$ contributes $Z_{i+1}^{1/s_i}$ before that power
is taken. Adding the current choice therefore gives
$(1+Z_{i+1}^{1/s_i})^{s_i}$. These successive sums explain the nested
functions below. A common power gives $Z_i=h_i^{s_i}$; different
powers retain the separate coordinate capacities. The ordered maximum
determines where the powers must coincide.

On the closed ordered simplex $1\geq s_1\geq\cdots\geq s_k\geq0$ put
\begin{align}
 G_k&=s_k\log2,&
 G_i&=s_i\log(1+\exp(G_{i+1}/s_i)),\\
 Z_i&=\exp G_i,&
 J(L;s)&=\sum_i L_i+\sum_j s_jV_j-\sum_i L_iZ_i.
 \label{profile:saddle}
\end{align}
At zero products use the continuous perspective extension. Let $s=s(L)$ be the unique maximizer of $J(L;s)$ on the ordered
simplex. Its existence and uniqueness are proved in
Section~\ref{paper:geometry}; Appendix~\ref{supp:ordered-saddle-scalar-elimination}
gives a scalar recursion for its evaluation. The geometric theorem supplies
\begin{equation}
 \tfrac12<s_k\leq s_1<1-\epsilon_H,
 \qquad \epsilon_H=\frac{2\log2-1}{2H(\log H)^2}.
 \label{profile:compact}
\end{equation}
In particular $1\leq Z_i\leq H$. A maximal interval $[a,b]$
on which $s_i$ is constant is called a plateau; denote its common
value by $\sigma$. A nonterminal plateau has $b<k$ and
$z=\exp(G_{b+1}/\sigma)$; the terminal plateau has $b=k$ and $z=1$.
The exterior names of this plateau are $a,\ldots,b$. Its local groups
are the original groups $i\in[a,b]$, of ranks $r_i=b-i+1$.
Original groups $g<a$ are its earlier groups, of rank $b-a+1$.
Each original group retains its own random clock.

In the divisor model, name $c$ is coordinate $d_c$: primes in group $i$
may be assigned to $c\geq i$, and $V_c$ is its deadline. Assignments to
coordinates beyond $b$, together with the unused primes, form the
plateau's compound child.

For $l<k$ define
\[
 \beta_l=\frac{\exp(G_{l+1}/s_l)}{1+\exp(G_{l+1}/s_l)}.
\]
The reference intensity per eligible exterior name is
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_g=
 \begin{cases}
 Z_g\displaystyle\prod_{l=g}^{a-1}\beta_l/(b-a+1+z),&g<a,\\
 (b-g+1+z)^{\sigma-1},&a\leq g\leq b.
 \end{cases}
 \label{profile:old-coefficients}
\end{equation}
The coefficients for the earlier groups are the intensities transported
along their routes into the plateau. We keep them separately to retain
the constraints at each deadline. Set
\[
 E_q(z)=(q+z)\log(q+z)-z\log z,\qquad
 g_g(q)=q-\kappa_gE_q(z).
\]

\subsection{The endpoint costs}
A binary comparison removes some exterior names and retains the
others, together with the compound child. The two ends of its time
interval have different available reserves. To calculate them, we
enumerate the legal choices for all the surrounding cuts; these are
the outside contexts. Only a finite list of contexts is needed because
each cut occurs at a group boundary.

For every local group $i$ enumerate the edges $r_i\to q$, where
$0\leq q<r_i$ for a nonterminal plateau, and $1\leq q<r_i$ for the terminal
plateau. The latter exclusion removes the degenerate ordinary edge.
The retained exterior names are $B=\{b-q+1,\ldots,b\}$; $B$ is empty
when $q=0$. The compound child is always retained.

For each edge, enumerate the outside contexts as follows.
For each name $c\in\{a,\ldots,i-1\}$ choose
$\tau_c\in\{V_0,\ldots,V_c\}$ independently. For each $c\in B$ choose
$\tau_c\in\{V_i,\ldots,V_c\}$ independently. In the left completion
set $\tau_c=V_{i-1}$ for all $i\leq c\leq b-q$; in the right completion
set those same cuts to $V_i$. All other cuts are identical in the two
completions. This gives a finite set of lawful pairs $(v^-,v^+)$.
Each cut lies before its coordinate's deadline, and the compound
child remains intact.

For either completion $v$ and original group $1\leq g\leq b$, let
\[
 A_{v,g}=\{c\in\{a,\ldots,b\}:\tau_c\geq V_g\},
 \qquad q_{v,g}=|A_{v,g}|,
 \qquad t_v=\max_{a\leq c\leq b}\tau_c.
\]
In an earlier group the shallowest eligible name is $a$, and in local
group $g$ it is $g$. Call $g$ good when $0<q_{v,g}<r_g$ and this
shallowest eligible name is absent from $A_{v,g}$. Define
\begin{equation}
 \overline C_v=\sum_{g\leq b}L_gg_g(q_{v,g}),\qquad
 S_{\mathrm{good}}(v)=\sum_{g\text{ good}}\sqrt{L_g}.
 \label{profile:reference}
\end{equation}
At the optimizer, the endpoint geometry gives $\overline C_v\geq0$,
with the coefficients and lengths of the earlier groups included.

For a nonterminal plateau put $T=\sum_{a\leq i\leq b}L_i$,
$d=\sigma/s_{b+1}-1$, and
\[
 \widehat R=1+\frac{\sqrt{1+T}}{1+d\sqrt{1+T}}.
\]
For the terminal plateau set $\widehat R=0$. Define
\begin{equation}
 S_v=\begin{cases}
 1+\widehat R+\overline C_v,&t_v\leq V_b/2,\\
 1+\overline C_v+S_{\mathrm{good}}(v),&t_v>V_b/2,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad X_e=\min_v S_{v^-},\quad Y_e=\min_v S_{v^+}.
 \label{profile:scores}
\end{equation}
The early score includes the uncertainty of a proper exit-count window.
At the late endpoint the incoming contribution cancels from the intrinsic
cost; the additional square-root terms instead measure the fluctuation
needed to remove an eligible shallow name while retaining deeper names.
The two minima are taken separately over the same finite set of paired
lawful contexts. The lower bound makes the two scores compatible by
keeping the actual type increment $\Delta$ fixed and choosing the legal pair
$x=\max(a_*X_e,a_*Y_e-\Delta)$, $y=x+\Delta$; see
\eqref{lower:local-pair}.

\subsection{Scalar persistence and canonical edge factors}
The path comparison has two sources of fluctuation: the prime
positions shared by all words and the private labels of the word being
summed. The following Gaussian model preserves this distinction.
The parameter $\rho$ is the fraction of variance supplied by the common
environment, and $\eta$ is the power at which its conditional survival
mass is averaged.

Let $E,W$ be independent stationary standard Ornstein--Uhlenbeck
processes, with covariance $e^{-|u-v|/2}$. For $0<\eta,\rho<1$ set
\begin{align}
 F_{\eta,\rho}(t)&=
 \mathbb E_E\Big[\mathbb P_W\{
 \sqrt\rho E_u+\sqrt{1-\rho}W_u\geq0\ (0\leq u\leq t)
 \mid E\}^{\eta}\Big],\\
 \chi(\eta,\rho)&=\lim_{t\to\infty}-t^{-1}\log F_{\eta,\rho}(t).
 \label{profile:chi}
\end{align}
Theorem~\ref{pr:gaussian} and
Propositions~\ref{pr:existence} and \ref{pr:lipschitz} give existence, local Lipschitz continuity,
and $\eta/2\leq\chi\leq1/2$. With $b(t)=-\log F_{\eta,\rho}(t)$,
the finite-time comparison gives a constant $C_Q$ on each compact
parameter set such that
\begin{equation}
 \frac{b(t)-\log C_Q}{t}\le\chi(\eta,\rho)\le\frac{b(t)}t.
 \label{profile:chi-bracket}
\end{equation}
Thus $\chi$ is characterized by
$C_Q^{-1}e^{-\chi t}\le F_{\eta,\rho}(t)\le e^{-\chi t}$ for all $t\ge0$.

For evaluating this function, Proposition~\ref{pr:existence} gives
the finite Gaussian grid rule, displaced thresholds, crossing control
and Gaussian translation error. Combine its finite-time enclosures with
\eqref{profile:chi-bracket}; Section~\ref{supp:explicit-ou-construction}
specifies $C_Q$ on a compact parameter set. Taking $t$ large and then
refining the Gaussian grid determines this two-variable function to
arbitrary prescribed accuracy. For $k=1$ the edge product is empty, so
$\chi$ is never evaluated at a degenerate parameter.

For $e=(i,r,q)$ put $a=\log(r+z)$, $b_e=\log(q+z)$,
$p=(q+z)/(r+z)$, and
\begin{equation}
 m=a-b_ep,\qquad
 \rho_e=\frac{m^2}{m^2+b_e^2p(1-p)},\qquad
 T_e=\frac{(1+X_e)(1+Y_e)}{1+(r+z)^\sigma L_i},\qquad
 P_e=\min(1,T_e)^{2\chi(\sigma,\rho_e)}.
 \label{profile:edge-factor}
\end{equation}
The binary laws are nondegenerate: a nonterminal zero-output edge
has $z>1$, and the terminal zero-output edge is excluded. The product
in \eqref{profile:raw} includes every canonical edge.

\subsection{The ordinary terminal suffix}
The terminal comparison leaves no compound child beyond the last
plateau. Its zero-output edge is therefore an ordinary one-channel
constraint, handled separately from the binary factors. The suffix
chosen below contains a fixed proportion of the total time and enough
drift to account for the preceding groups. Its exact count and path
constraint together give one factor.

Here $h_i=k-i+2$ on the complete original chain. If the selected suffix
starts at group $j$, then $V_{\rm pre}=V_{j-1}$ includes all preceding
plateaux as well as the earlier terminal groups.
For $2\leq h\leq H$ define
\[
 \alpha_h=\frac{\log((h-1)/\log h)}{\log h},\quad
 c_w=\frac1{4H^2},\quad
 \tau=\min\left\{\frac14,\frac{c_w}{2H(\log H)^2},
 \frac14\min_{2\leq h<H}(\alpha_{h+1}-\alpha_h)\right\}.
\]
The thresholds $\alpha_h$ are strictly increasing. If the terminal
product $\sigma$ lies in $[\alpha_{h_i}-\tau,\alpha_{h_i}+\tau]$ for
a terminal local group, begin the suffix at that group; at most one
qualifies. Otherwise begin at the first terminal local group with
$e_i=h_i^\sigma\log h_i-(h_i-1)>0$. The KKT theorem ensures existence.
Let $U$ be the suffix length, $M$ its largest original block, and $A,B$
the total lengths before and after that block within the suffix. Break
largest-block ties at the earliest index. Put
\begin{equation}
 D=\sum_{i\text{ in suffix}}e_iL_i,\qquad
 \mathcal B(L)=\frac1{\sqrt{1+U}}
       \min\left\{1,\frac{(1+B)(1+D+A)}{1+M}\right\}.
 \label{profile:ordinary}
\end{equation}
Here $D\geq0$, and the suffix theorem gives $D\geq c_kV_{\rm pre}$
and $U\geq c_kV_k$. This is the sole ordinary root factor.

The positive-length raw expression is
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_k(L)=e^{-J(L;s(L))}\mathcal B(L)
 \prod_{j\text{ proper}}(1+d_j\sqrt{1+T_j})^{-\sigma_j}
 \prod_{e\text{ canonical}}P_e.
 \label{profile:raw}
\end{equation}
The saddle, plateaux and endpoint costs in this expression are evaluated
at $L$. The final formula uses $L^*$ as in \eqref{profile:final}.
There are at most $H^{2H}$ contexts for each of at most $kH$
canonical edges, and the scalar evaluator has depth $k$.


\subsection{A heuristic for the profile}
\label{profile:heuristic}

We now explain why both count and path costs enter
\eqref{profile:raw}. The discussion concerns the positive-length
Poisson core. The Gaussian model below predicts the binary exponent;
the exact bridge and arithmetic estimates are needed to make that
prediction uniform.

\paragraph{A count model and its missing constraints.}
In the Poisson model of the harmonic prime measure, take independent
counts $n_i\sim\Pois(L_i)$. There are
$\prod_i h_i^{n_i}$ routing words, whereas the available logarithmic
volume has scale $\exp(\sum_jV_j)$. A first model treats the words
as if they covered this volume without clustering. Dividing the
word count by this capacity and capping at $1$ gives its normalized
volume. The bound $\min(1,t)\le t^\alpha$ yields
\[
 \mathbb E\min\left\{1,
       e^{\sum_i n_i\log h_i-\sum_jV_j}\right\}
 \le
 \exp\left\{-\sum_iL_i-\alpha\sum_jV_j
                  +\sum_iL_ih_i^\alpha\right\},
 \qquad 0\le\alpha\le1.
\]
The exponent on the right is $-J(L;\alpha,\ldots,\alpha)$.
Optimizing it balances the supply of words against volume and tilts
the means to $L_ih_i^\alpha$. The full recursion
\eqref{profile:saddle} makes this balance at successive coordinates.
At its optimizer, Proposition~\ref{fp:prop:poisson} identifies $J$
with the Poisson entropy $\sum_iL_i\mathcal Q(Z_i)$.

The count model loses two kinds of information. Even with the right
total number of words, too many choices may lie in the same
coordinate projection. Moreover, the prime positions can force
clustering at an intermediate cut despite admissible endpoint counts.
Ford's dyadic heuristic \cite{FordDyadic2008} already explains the
second loss. Koukoulopoulos's first rectangular heuristic includes
an ordinary clustering correction; his further analysis
\cite[Section~2.2, Lemma~2.3 and Remark~2.4]{Kouk} identifies additional
projected-volume constraints.

The first loss can change the exponential scale. A stationary
common-power candidate only balances the sum of the coordinate
derivatives, whereas ordered optimality requires every proper
prefix sum to be nonpositive; see \eqref{hier:eq:KKT}. For example,
for $k\ge2$ take $L_1=T$, $L_k=cT$ and fixed intermediate lengths, with $c>0$
chosen so that the common-power stationary parameter tends to a fixed
$\alpha$ as $T\to\infty$. At this candidate,
\[
 \sum_{j<k}\partial_jJ
 =T\left[(k-1)-(k+1)^{\alpha-1}
       \{(k+1)\log(k+1)-2\log2\}\right]+o(T).
\]
This is the coefficient appearing in the obstruction
\cite[inequality~(2.13)]{Kouk}, with fixed shifts of the lengths
irrelevant to the leading comparison. When the coefficient is strictly positive,
increasing the first $k-1$ powers improves $J$ for large $T$.
Thus a single power overestimates the leading volume, and the ordered
saddle must split. The endpoint corrections below address the path
losses that remain after the saddle has been chosen.

\paragraph{The count windows and endpoint reserves.}
On a proper plateau of length $T$, central counts fluctuate on
scale $\sqrt T$. The exit likelihood penalizes a positive carry on scale
$d^{-1}$; see \eqref{paper:ep-likelihood-cancel}. Up to the fixed
reserve floor, the useful width is therefore
$\min(\sqrt T,d^{-1})$. Its fraction of the central count mass is
\[
 w\asymp(1+d\sqrt{1+T})^{-1}.
\]
The mixed-moment calculation contributes $w$ from count acceptance
and $w^{\sigma-1}$ from the inverse weight, giving $w^\sigma$;
see \eqref{lower:type-mass}--\eqref{lower:plateau-cost}.
The transition is controlled by $d\sqrt{1+T}$, so a small gap alone
does not remove the window cost.

The reference cost $\overline C_v$ is the margin between a lawful
cut's logarithmic capacity and its reference word entropy.
This margin supplies a path reserve. At an early context of a proper
plateau, the exit-count uncertainty supplies an additional reserve; at a late
end, removing a shallow name while retaining deeper names can use
a square-root label fluctuation. These are the extra terms in
\eqref{profile:scores}. Taking the most restrictive lawful cuts
gives $X_e,Y_e$. They are separately minimized scores; the
compatible-pair construction in \eqref{lower:local-pair} is needed
to realize a legal endpoint pair at those scales on one exact count fiber.

\paragraph{Why the binary power is $2\chi$.}
For an edge, use $a,b_e,p,m$ from \eqref{profile:edge-factor}.
A near-critical contrast has two fluctuation channels: the common
prime positions, with variance scale $m^2$, and the private
retained-label count, with variance scale $b_e^2p(1-p)$. Their
Gaussian variance ratio predicts $\rho_e$. This is a Gaussian
separation of the channels, rather than an assertion of independence
of the two physical-time counting processes.

Normalize the total variance and model the contrast as a linear
chord from $x>0$ to $y>0$ plus two independent centered Brownian
bridges of length $n$, with weights $\sqrt\rho,\sqrt{1-\rho}$.
A centered bridge has the representation in law
$\beta(t)=(n-t)B_{t/(n-t)}/\sqrt n$, where $B$ is standard
Brownian motion. The time change $v=t/(n-t)$, followed by $u=\log v$, turns its
nonnegative-path condition into
\[
 \sqrt\rho\,X_u+\sqrt{1-\rho}\,Y_u
 \ge -\frac{x}{\sqrt n}e^{-u/2}
      -\frac{y}{\sqrt n}e^{u/2},
\]
where $X,Y$ are independent stationary standard OU processes.
The two boundary terms become of order one at
$u=2\log(x/\sqrt n)$ and $u=2\log(\sqrt n/y)$.
When $xy<n$, the effective OU interval between these points has
length $2\log(n/(xy))$. The exponential boundary terms have bounded
OU action on this interval, so Lemma~\ref{pr:wall} changes the
zero-wall moment only by a constant factor. Thus conditional
persistence predicts
\[
 \exp\{-\chi(\sigma,\rho)[2\log(n/(xy))]_+\}
 =\min\{1,(xy/n)^{2\chi(\sigma,\rho)}\}.
\]
The endpoint product and the factor $2$ come from this time change;
very unequal reserves shift the interval without changing its length.
Putting $n$ on scale $(r+z)^\sigma L_i$ and restoring fixed reserve
floors gives $P_e$. Theorem~\ref{bridge:all-reserves} proves the
discrete comparison, and \eqref{lower:natural-correlation} justifies
the use of the reference parameter $\rho_e$ on the rare branch.

The order of averaging is essential here. In this Gaussian model,
let $q$ be the private survival mass conditional on the environment.
The plateau power gives
$\mathbb E q^\sigma$, with rate $\chi(\sigma,\rho)$.
Replacing it by $(\mathbb E q)^\sigma$ would give the ordinary
OU rate $\sigma/2$. The strict gap in
Proposition~\ref{pr:strict-annealing} shows that this substitution loses
a power when the effective interval grows. The canonical factors
are assembled by the conditional cover and intersection estimates;
their product does not assert independence of all cut events.

\paragraph{One terminal atom and one ordinary bridge.}
The terminal constant-mark constraint has no private binary channel.
Its count atom costs $(1+U)^{-1/2}$. Conditional on that same count,
the ordered drift supplies two ballot reserves, of scales $1+B$
and $1+D+A$. With $M$ the longest block, the remaining path cost is
$\min\{1,(1+B)(1+D+A)/(1+M)\}$.
The minimum also covers suffixes whose outward drift makes survival
a constant cost. These two costs give $\mathcal B(L)$;
Theorem~\ref{bridge:ordinary-root} estimates them jointly.
There is one root atom, rather than one atom for each group.
For $k=1$, $\mathcal B(L)=(1+L_1)^{-3/2}$: a count-only prediction
sees the square-root atom but misses the additional inverse-length
loss from clustering. This is the ordinary barrier loss in Ford's
dyadic formula. In higher dimensions, the binary factors retain
the analogous losses in the conditional label mass.

\subsection{Reading and evaluating the profile}
\label{profile:reading}

Formula~\eqref{profile:raw} separates the leading count cost from the
corrections caused by overlap. The exponential of the saddle value
pays for the tilted counts. Each proper plateau boundary contributes
its count window, with the power of the plateau from which it exits.
Each canonical edge contributes the survival cost calculated from its
two endpoint scores. The factor $\mathcal B(L)$ contains both the
ordinary count atom and the terminal path constraint; neither is
inserted a second time elsewhere in the profile.

The calculation proceeds from the lengths to the ordered saddle, then
to its plateaux, the finite endpoint lists, and the displayed factors.
The scalar recursion in
Appendix~\ref{supp:ordered-saddle-scalar-elimination} evaluates the
saddle without a separate search over plateau patterns. The only
universal function to approximate is $\chi$; its finite-time enclosure
is \eqref{profile:chi-bracket}. Thus the definition is the same for all
rectangles in a fixed dimension, including those whose active
constraints change as the lengths vary.

For reference, the principal quantities are collected here. Their
precise definitions and hypotheses are in the indicated sections.
\begin{longtable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.23\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.69\textwidth}}
\toprule
Quantity & Meaning and definition \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead
\toprule
Quantity & Meaning and definition \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endfoot
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
$L_i$, $V_i$ & Length of prime group $i$ on the logarithmic clock, and its cumulative deadline; Sections~\ref{paper:arithmetic-setup} and \ref{profile:definition}. \\
$s(L)$, $\sigma$ & Ordered saddle coordinates, and the common coordinate on a plateau; \eqref{profile:saddle}. \\
$Z_i$, $\kappa_g$ & Tilted group intensity, and reference intensity per exterior name reaching a plateau; \eqref{profile:saddle} and \eqref{profile:old-coefficients}. \\
$\overline C_v$, $S_v$ & Reference cost and endpoint score of a lawful context; \eqref{profile:reference} and \eqref{profile:scores}. \\
$X_e$, $Y_e$ & The left and right endpoint scores used for canonical edge $e$; \eqref{profile:scores}. \\
$\chi(\eta,\rho)$, $P_e$ & Conditional survival exponent and its canonical binary factor; \eqref{profile:chi} and \eqref{profile:edge-factor}. \\
$\mathcal B(L)$ & Ordinary suffix factor, including its exact count atom; \eqref{profile:ordinary}. \\
$K_k(\ell)$ & Normalized harmonic volume sum at the given cutoffs; \eqref{paper:K}. \\
$\Psi_k(L)$, $\Phi_k(\ell)$ & Positive-length profile and its extension by the fixed lift; \eqref{profile:raw} and \eqref{profile:final}. \\
\end{longtable}

\subsection{Two worked profiles}
\label{profile:examples}

The following examples evaluate the factors in \eqref{profile:raw}
in two different regimes. The first has comparable prime ranges and
a positive ordinary drift. The second has a strict saddle separation
and a binary factor which changes the power of the logarithmic clock.
All lengths are at least the fixed lift threshold. They correspond
to actual ordered cutoffs by taking
$y_i=\exp\{(\log3)e^{V_i}\}$; hence the lift is inactive and
Theorem~\ref{new:main} gives $H^{(k+1)}(x,\mathbf y,2\mathbf y)
\asymp_k x\Psi_k(L)$ for $x\ge2^k(y_1\cdots y_k)y_k$.
Likewise, Theorem~\ref{table:main} gives
$A_{k+1}(\mathbf N)\asymp_k(\prod_iN_i)\Psi_k(L)$ when
$N_i=2y_i$ for $i\le k$ and $N_{k+1}\ge2y_k$.

\begin{example}[Two comparable prime ranges]\label{profile:example-two}
Let $k=2$ and $L_1=L_2=T\to\infty$. The saddle has one plateau,
$s_1=s_2=\sigma$, where
\[
 3^\sigma\log3+2^\sigma\log2=3,
 \qquad \alpha_2<\sigma<\alpha_3.
\]
Indeed, this equation gives stationarity along the equality face.
Its proper prefix derivative is
$T\{1-3^{\sigma-1}(3\log3-2\log2)\}<0$, so the ordered KKT
condition holds. The sign follows already at $\alpha_2$ from
$3^{\alpha_2-1}(3\log3-2\log2)>1$ and is preserved as $\sigma$
increases. Strict concavity identifies the saddle.

Put $c_1=1-2\cdot3^{\sigma-1}\log2$ and
$c_2=2-3^\sigma\log3=2^\sigma\log2-1$.
The only binary edge is $2\to1$ in group $1$. Its retained name $2$
has cut $T$ or $2T$: the former is early, at $t_v=V_2/2$, and
the latter is late. The corresponding left scores are
$1+c_1T$ and $1+(c_1-c_2)T+\sqrt T$; the right scores are
$1+c_2T$ and $1$. Thus
\[
 X=1+\min\{c_1T,(c_1-c_2)T+\sqrt T\},\qquad Y=1.
\]
Here $c_1>c_2>0$. For example, rigorous scalar brackets give
$0.54133<\sigma<0.54134$, $0.1624<c_1<0.1625$, and
$0.0087<c_2<0.0088$. In \eqref{profile:edge-factor},
$a=\log3$, $b_e=\log2$, $p=2/3$, and $\eta=\sigma$.
Consequently $T_e\to2(c_1-c_2)/3^\sigma>0$ and $P_e\asymp1$:
the linear left reserve compensates for the bounded right reserve.

For $H=3$, the thresholds satisfy $\alpha_2<0.52877$,
$\alpha_3>0.54532$, and $\tau<0.00384$; thus $\sigma$ is outside
both bands in the ordinary-suffix rule. The suffix is therefore
group $2$, with $U=M=T$, $A=B=0$, and $D=c_2T$. There is no
proper exit window. Writing $I_2=2+3\sigma-3^\sigma-2^\sigma$, we obtain
\[
 \mathcal B(L)=\frac{1+c_2T}{(1+T)^{3/2}},\qquad
 \Psi_2(T,T)\asymp e^{-I_2T}T^{-1/2}.
\]
Positive drift makes the ordinary path cost bounded away from zero;
only its single count atom supplies a power of $T$. The zero-drift
balanced case in Section~\ref{assembly:special-cases} has the
additional inverse-length path cost.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[A strict separation with a conditional power]
\label{profile:example-split}
Let $k=6$, fix $\lambda\ge\max\{1,\Lambda_6\}$, and take
$L=(T,\lambda,\lambda,\lambda,\lambda,100T)$ as $T\to\infty$.
On the face $s_1=\cdots=s_5$, $J/T$ tends to the objective of
the two-node chain $(h_1,h_2)=(7,2)$,
with multiplicities $(5,1)$ and lengths $(1,100)$.
It has products $\sigma_0>\tau_0$, characterized by
\begin{equation}\label{profile:example-split-equations}
 \begin{gathered}
 z_0=2^{\tau_0/\sigma_0},\qquad
 5=(5+z_0)^{\sigma_0-1}E_5(z_0),\\
 101=\log2\{100\cdot2^{\tau_0}
                    +z_0(5+z_0)^{\sigma_0-1}\}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
To verify the strict separation, set
$\theta=1+\log(5/E_5(2))/\log7$. Then
$\alpha_2<\theta<\alpha_7$ and
\[
 c_*:=\frac{6-7^\theta\log7}{2^\theta\log2-1}
 \quad\hbox{satisfies}\quad 54<c_*<55.
\]
Since $100>c_*$, the stationary common power $\alpha$ is below
$\theta$. Its first node derivative
$5-7^{\alpha-1}E_5(2)$ is then positive, violating ordered KKT.
The unique two-node saddle therefore splits and satisfies
\eqref{profile:example-split-equations}. The global bounds give
$\alpha_2<\tau_0<\sigma_0<1$.

Put $g(q)=q-(5+z_0)^{\sigma_0-1}E_q(z_0)$.
The first equation gives $g(0)=g(5)=0$; strict concavity gives
$g(q)>0$ for $0<q<5$. The complete-chain prefix derivatives,
divided by $T$, tend to $-g(5-j)<0$ at $j=1,\ldots,4$.
These KKT signs identify the full limiting saddle: all four
internal constraints are active and the gap after group $5$ is strict.
The nonsingular two-variable Hessian gives face-critical products
$\sigma_T=\sigma_0+O_\lambda(T^{-1})$ and
$\tau_T=\tau_0+O_\lambda(T^{-1})$.
The strict signs and gap persist, so these are the actual saddle
products for large $T$, with plateaux $[1,5]$ and $[6,6]$.

The critical binary edge is $5\to0$ in group $1$. It has one
context pair: all five cuts are $0$ on the left and $T$ on the right.
For $T>4\lambda$, the left context is early and the right context
is late, with no good groups. With $z_T=2^{\tau_T/\sigma_T}$ and
$g_{1,T}(q)=q-(5+z_T)^{\sigma_T-1}E_q(z_T)$, the exact scores are
\[
 X=1+\widehat R,\qquad Y=1+Tg_{1,T}(5),\qquad
 Tg_{1,T}(5)=-\lambda\sum_{r=1}^4
       \{r-(r+z_T)^{\sigma_T-1}E_r(z_T)\}=O_\lambda(1).
\]
Here $\widehat R$ uses the plateau length $T+4\lambda$.
The last identity is the top plateau balance; reference
nonnegativity also gives $Y\ge1$. Since
$d_T=\sigma_T/\tau_T-1\to d_0>0$, both scores are bounded.
Hence $T_e\asymp_\lambda T^{-1}$ and
$P_e\asymp_\lambda T^{-2\chi(\sigma_0,\rho_0)}$, where
\[
 p_0=\frac{z_0}{5+z_0},\quad
 m_0=\log(5+z_0)-p_0\log z_0,\quad
 \rho_0=\frac{m_0^2}{m_0^2+(\log z_0)^2p_0(1-p_0)}\in(0,1).
\]
Local Lipschitz continuity of $\chi$ justifies replacing its
$T$-dependent parameters by these limits. For each other edge in
group $1$, its left reference cost is $Tg(q)+O_\lambda(1)$ with
$1\le q<5$, so its factor is bounded below. Every remaining binary
edge has the fixed length $\lambda$ and factor at least
$\min\{1,4/(1+7\lambda)\}$. All these factors are therefore
comparable to $1$.

The proper window contributes $T^{-\sigma_0/2}$. The ordinary
suffix consists of group $6$: $U=M=100T$, $A=B=0$, and
$D=(2^{\tau_T}\log2-1)100T$. Its drift is strictly positive
because $\tau_0>\alpha_2$, so $\mathcal B(L)\asymp T^{-1/2}$.
Finally, with
$I_{100}=Q((5+z_0)^{\sigma_0})+100Q(2^{\tau_0})$, the entropy
identity gives $J=I_{100}T+O_\lambda(1)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{profile:example-split-result}
 \boxed{\ \Psi_6(L)\asymp_\lambda
 e^{-I_{100}T}
 T^{-1/2-\sigma_0/2-2\chi(\sigma_0,\rho_0)}\ }.
\end{equation}
The three powers record the ordinary atom, the proper exit window,
and the conditional binary bridge. Proposition~\ref{pr:strict-annealing}
gives $2\chi(\sigma_0,\rho_0)>\sigma_0$; averaging the private
survival before taking its plateau power would therefore miss a
strictly positive power of $T$ in this family.
\end{example}

\section{Geometry of the ordered saddle}\label{sec:geometry}\label{paper:geometry}

The ordered saddle determines both the exponential cost of supplying
prime factors and the constraints that remain after this cost has been
paid. Equal consecutive products form plateaux. Each strict separation
between plateaux introduces a count window whose width depends on the
product gap; within a plateau, the stationarity margins provide the
reserves for the path estimates.
We therefore need more than existence of an optimizer: the argument
requires uniform control of its curvature, its local drifts, and the
relative lengths of its plateaux.

The proof has three stages. First, the recursive objective is concave,
and each term has enough curvature to control all later products.
Boundary variations then place the unique optimizer in a fixed compact
region. Second, the stationarity equations identify the node margins
and center the uncolored root exactly. Third, a positive entropy surplus
across each strict separation forces a length hierarchy. This hierarchy
supplies a long block in which a single Poisson count can impose the
root condition, even when the final original block is short.

We treat a general finite rank chain before specializing to the complete
chain of the divisor problem. The generality is needed when equalities
are imposed during changes of parameters.

\subsection{The objective and the main conclusions}

Fix integers
\[
 H=h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\ge 2,
\]
where the one-element chain is allowed.  Set
\[
 p_i=h_i-h_{i+1}\quad(i<m),\qquad p_m=h_m-1,
 \qquad V_j=\sum_{i=1}^j L_i,\quad V_0=0,
\]
with arbitrary \(L_i>0\).  The symbols \(p_i\) always denote these
positive integers.  Child probabilities will instead be denoted by
\(\beta_i\).

On the ordered simplex
\[
 \calD=\{s\in\R^m:1\ge s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_m\ge0\}
\]
define, first at positive products,
\begin{align}
 G_m(s)&=s_m\log h_m,\nonumber\\
 G_i(s)&=s_i\log\bigl(p_i+\exp(G_{i+1}(s)/s_i)\bigr)
                   &&(i<m),\label{geom:eq:recursion}\\
 Z_i(s)&=\exp G_i(s),\nonumber\\
 J(L;s)&=\sum_iL_i+\sum_j s_jp_jV_j-\sum_iL_iZ_i(s).
                                                        \label{geom:eq:objective}
\end{align}
Use the continuous extension at zero products.  Indeed, induction gives
\(0\le G_i(s)\le s_i\log h_i\): if
\(G_{i+1}\le s_{i+1}\log h_{i+1}\), ordering gives
\(\exp(G_{i+1}/s_i)\le h_{i+1}\).  Thus when \(s_i=0\) its whole
suffix is zero and \(G_i=0\), \(Z_i=1\).  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 1\le Z_i(s)\le h_i \qquad(s\in\calD).             \label{geom:eq:globalZ}
\end{equation}

For \(E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\), let
\[
 \calD_E=\{s\in\calD:s_j=s_{j+1}\text{ for every }j\in E\}.
\]
Write \(s^E(L)\) for the maximizer on \(\calD_E\) and
\(J_E^*(L)=J(L;s^E(L))\). The constraints defining \(\calD\) remain
in force, and additional equalities may occur at the maximizer.
The next theorem gives existence and uniqueness.

Throughout, \(c,C>0\) may change from line to line and depend only on
the fixed chain.  In particular they do not depend on \(L\), its ratios,
the face \(E\), or the sizes of product gaps and multipliers.  The notation
\(A\asymp B\) means \(cB\le A\le CB\), with this convention.

\begin{theorem}[Global bounds]\label{geom:thm:global}
Put
\begin{equation}
 c_0=2\log2-1,\qquad
 \varepsilon_H=\frac{c_0}{2H(\log H)^2}.             \label{geom:eq:epsilon}
\end{equation}
For every positive length vector and every \(E\), there is a unique
maximizer on \(\calD_E\), and it satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \frac12<s_m^E(L)\le s_1^E(L)<1-\varepsilon_H.
                                                        \label{geom:eq:outer}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Concavity and the outer boundaries}

Continuity on the compact ordered simplex gives existence. To prove
uniform interiority,
we vary the entire top or bottom plateau, so that every prescribed
equality is respected. The bottom variation compares the linear budget
with the cost of increasing the final alphabets; the top variation uses
a definite entropy excess near product one.

The map \(x\mapsto\log(p+e^x)\) is convex and increasing.  Its
perspective \((s,y)\mapsto s\log(p+e^{y/s})\) is convex for \(s>0\)
and is increasing in \(y\).  Induction in \eqref{geom:eq:recursion} therefore
shows that each \(G_i\), and hence each \(Z_i\), is convex.  The continuous
extension gives convexity on \(\calD\).  Thus \(J\) is concave and
continuous on the compact convex set \(\calD_E\), so a maximum exists.

\subsubsection{The bottom plateau}

\begin{lemma}\label{geom:lem:bottom}
Every maximizer on \(\calD_E\) satisfies \(s_m>1/2\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If the maximal bottom block \(a,\ldots,m\) has common product
\(\sigma\le1/2\), we can raise the whole block. When \(a>1\),
maximality makes the preceding gap strict, so this variation respects
all prescribed equalities. Inside the block the recursion telescopes
exactly:
\[
 G_i=\sigma\log h_i,\qquad Z_i=h_i^\sigma\quad(i\ge a).
\]
For \(i<a\), set
\[
 \beta_i=\frac{\exp(G_{i+1}/s_i)}
                    {p_i+\exp(G_{i+1}/s_i)}.
\]
Along this bottom-block direction,
\[
 \frac{dG_i}{d\sigma}
   =\left(\prod_{i\le b<a}\beta_b\right)\log h_a.
\]
The identity
\[
 Z_i\beta_i=Z_{i+1}\beta_i^{\,1-s_i}
\]
implies
\[
 Z_i\prod_{i\le b<a}\beta_b
   = Z_a\prod_{i\le b<a}\beta_b^{\,1-s_b}\le Z_a.
\]
When \(\sigma=0\), all preceding products, if present, are positive,
and these formulas give the right derivative.  There are no preceding
terms if \(a=1\).

The derivative of the linear budget is
\[
 \sum_{j\ge a}p_jV_j
   =(h_a-1)V_{a-1}+\sum_{i\ge a}(h_i-1)L_i.
\]
Consequently the directional derivative of \(J\) is at least
\begin{equation}
 V_{a-1}(h_a-1-h_a^\sigma\log h_a)
       +\sum_{i\ge a}L_i(h_i-1-h_i^\sigma\log h_i). \label{geom:eq:bottomderivative}
\end{equation}
For every real \(h>1\), one has \(\sqrt h\log h<h-1\).
Indeed, with \(t=\sqrt h\), the difference
\(t^2-1-2t\log t\) vanishes at \(1\) and has positive derivative
\(2(t-1-\log t)\) for \(t>1\).
Every bracket in \eqref{geom:eq:bottomderivative} is thus positive.
Since the lengths are positive, the derivative is strictly positive.
This contradicts maximality, including at \(\sigma=0\).
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The top plateau}

\begin{lemma}\label{geom:lem:top}
Every maximizer on \(\calD_E\) satisfies \(s_1<1-\varepsilon_H\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(1,\ldots,b\) be the maximal top equal-product block, with
common value \(\sigma\).  If \(b<m\), put
\(C=h_{b+1}\) and \(z=\exp(G_{b+1}/\sigma)\); otherwise put \(C=z=1\).
For \(i\le b\), let \(n_i=h_i-C\ge1\).  Telescoping yields
\[
 G_i=\sigma\log(n_i+z).
\]
Here \(1\le z\le C\) and \(n_i+z\le H\), by the ordered recursion.
Varying the top block while keeping its child products fixed gives
\begin{equation}
 \frac{dZ_i}{d\sigma}=(n_i+z)^\sigma A(n_i,z),\qquad
 A(n,z)=\log(n+z)-\frac{z\log z}{n+z}.             \label{geom:eq:topderivative}
\end{equation}
This formula includes the variation of \(z=\exp(G_{b+1}/\sigma)\).
The budget derivative is \(\sum_{i\le b}L_i n_i\).

Write
\[
 E_n(z)=(n+z)\log(n+z)-z\log z=(n+z)A(n,z).
\]
It is increasing in \(z\), since \(\partial_zE_n=\log(1+n/z)>0\).
Moreover
\[
 E_n(z)\ge E_n(1)=(n+1)\log(n+1)\ge2n\log2.
\]
For the last inequality,
\((n+1)\log(n+1)/n\) is increasing for \(n>0\), with derivative
\([n-\log(n+1)]/n^2>0\), and \(n\ge1\).
Also \(0<A(n,z)\le\log H\).  With \(n,z\) fixed at their values
at the point under consideration, for \(0\le\tau\le1\),
\[
 \frac{d}{d\tau}\bigl((n+z)^\tau A(n,z)\bigr)
 \le H(\log H)^2.
\]
This auxiliary comparison keeps \(z\) fixed.
If \(\sigma\ge1-\varepsilon_H\), it follows that
\[
 (n+z)^\sigma A(n,z)-n
 \ge n(2\log2-1)-\varepsilon_HH(\log H)^2
 \ge c_0/2>0.
\]
Thus raising the top block has strictly negative derivative for \(J\).
Lowering it a sufficiently small amount is feasible and increases
\(J\), a contradiction.  This also covers \(\sigma=1\).
\end{proof}

Let \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_H\), which lies in \((0,1/2)\), and put
\[
 \calD_\varepsilon
   =\{s:\varepsilon\le s_m\le\cdots\le s_1\le1-\varepsilon\}.
\]
The preceding lemmas put every maximizer on every prescribed face in
this single compact set.  We will use differential estimates on the
slightly larger convex set \(\calD_{\varepsilon/2}\).

\subsection{Full suffix curvature and uniqueness}

Convexity alone would allow flat maximizing directions. The stronger
fact needed here is that a single recursive term controls every
coordinate on which it depends. The derivative recursion below separates
the motion at the current node from the motion transmitted by its child;
neither can vanish unless the whole suffix direction vanishes. Summing
these estimates with the original length weights gives the natural
cumulative-length scale for the Hessian.

For \(i<m\), introduce
\[
 a_i=G_i/s_i=\log S_i,\qquad
 u_i=s_{i+1}/s_i,\qquad
 \beta_i=\frac{e^{G_{i+1}/s_i}}{S_i},\qquad
 A_i=a_i-u_i\beta_i a_{i+1},
\]
where \(S_i=p_i+e^{G_{i+1}/s_i}\); set
\(a_m=A_m=\log h_m\).
All these functions and the derivatives needed below are bounded on
\(\calD_{\varepsilon/2}\).  The quantities \(s_i,a_i,\beta_i,1-\beta_i\)
have positive chain-dependent lower bounds.  The same holds for \(A_i\):
it is the entropy of the distribution consisting of \(p_i\) named
probabilities \(1/S_i\) and the one compound probability \(\beta_i\).
These assertions use compactness but no separation of adjacent products.

\begin{lemma}[One perspective term controls its entire suffix]
\label{geom:lem:suffix}
For any \(s\in\calD_{\varepsilon/2}\), direction \(z\in\R^m\), and \(i\),
\begin{equation}
 c\sum_{j\ge i}z_j^2\le D^2Z_i(s)[z,z]
                   \le C\sum_{j\ge i}z_j^2.      \label{geom:eq:suffix}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We prove the lower and upper curvature bounds together by propagating
the first and second variations down the recursion. Write
\(g_i=DG_i[z]\) and \(Q_i=D^2G_i[z,z]\). Differentiation gives
\begin{align}
 g_m&=(\log h_m)z_m,\qquad Q_m=0,\nonumber\\
 g_i&=A_i z_i+\beta_i g_{i+1},\nonumber\\
 Q_i&=\beta_iQ_{i+1}
  +\frac{\beta_i(1-\beta_i)}{s_i}
              (g_{i+1}-u_i a_{i+1}z_i)^2.        \label{geom:eq:perspectivecurvature}
\end{align}
In particular \(Q_i\ge0\).  Put \(E_i=g_i^2+Q_i\) and
\(w_i=g_{i+1}-u_i a_{i+1}z_i\).  Then
\[
 g_i=a_i z_i+\beta_iw_i,\qquad
 Q_i\ge c w_i^2+cQ_{i+1}.
\]
Thus \(z_i^2\le CE_i\), and then \(g_{i+1}^2\le CE_i\), so that
\(E_{i+1}\le CE_i\).  Iteration over the fixed number of indices,
starting with \(E_m=(\log h_m)^2z_m^2\), proves
\[
 E_i\ge c\sum_{j\ge i}z_j^2.
\]
The same recursion gives the upper bound, since all coefficients in
\eqref{geom:eq:perspectivecurvature} are bounded. Passing from the
logarithm to its exponential uses
\[
 D^2Z_i[z,z]=Z_iE_i,
\]
and \(Z_i\) is bounded above and below.
\end{proof}

Define the negative objective Hessian by
\(\calH(L;s)=-D_s^2J(L;s)\).
Summing \eqref{geom:eq:suffix} with weights \(L_i\) gives
\begin{equation}
 c\sum_jV_j z_j^2
 \le z^{\mathsf T}\calH(L;s)z
 \le C\sum_jV_j z_j^2.                            \label{geom:eq:hessian}
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}
 |\calH_{ij}(L;s)|\le C V_{\min(i,j)},             \label{geom:eq:hessianentry}
\end{equation}
because only terms \(L_\ell Z_\ell\) with \(\ell\le\min(i,j)\)
depend on both coordinates, and their second derivatives are bounded.
These estimates hold for every positive length vector, without
stationarity or a length hierarchy.

To conclude uniqueness, suppose two distinct points maximize on
\(\calD_E\). Concavity makes their connecting segment maximizing.
The boundary lemmas place this segment in \(\calD_\varepsilon\),
where \eqref{geom:eq:hessian} gives strict concavity along every
nonzero direction. The contradiction completes
Theorem~\ref{geom:thm:global}.

\subsection{The finite optimization and its product bounds}

We now express the same optimization in node notation, which makes
the routing probabilities and stationarity equations explicit. Retain
\[
 H=h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\ge2,
 \qquad p_j=h_j-h_{j+1}\ (j<m),\qquad p_m=h_m-1.
\]
Let $L_i>0$, $V_j=\sum_{i\le j}L_i$, and $V_0=0$. Write the ordered
simplex as
\[
 \mathcal S=\{1\ge s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots\ge s_m\ge0\}.
\]
For positive products define recursively
\begin{align}
 G_m&=s_m\log h_m,&
 G_j&=s_j\log\bigl(p_j+\exp(G_{j+1}/s_j)\bigr)\quad(j<m),
 \label{hier:eq:G}\\
 Z_j&=e^{G_j},&
 J(\mathbf s)&=\sum_iL_i+\sum_j s_jp_jV_j-\sum_iL_iZ_i.
 \label{hier:eq:J}
\end{align}
The extension to $\mathcal S$ is the one used above: when $s_j=0$,
the whole suffix has zero product and $G_j=0$. The bound
$0\le G_j\le s_j\log h_j$ proves continuity on these faces.
Compactness gives existence. The convex, increasing perspective of
$y\mapsto\log(p+e^y)$ makes each $G_j$ and then each $Z_j$
convex on $\mathcal S$, so $J$ is concave. Henceforth the optimizer
is the unique one of Theorem~\ref{geom:thm:global}.

When products are positive, put
\begin{align}
 S_m&=h_m,& S_j&=p_j+S_{j+1}^{u_j},&u_j&=s_{j+1}/s_j,\\
 \beta_j&=S_{j+1}^{u_j}/S_j,&
 A_j&=\log S_j-u_j\beta_j\log S_{j+1}\quad(j<m),&
 A_m&=\log h_m. \label{hier:eq:node}
\end{align}
Then $G_j=s_j\log S_j$, $Z_j=S_j^{s_j}$, and
$2\le S_j\le h_j\le H$. We repeatedly use the entropy increment
\begin{equation}
 E_n(z)=(n+z)\log(n+z)-z\log z,
 \qquad n>0,\ z\ge1. \label{hier:eq:entropy}
\end{equation}
For a nonterminal node, $A_j=E_{p_j}(S_{j+1}^{u_j})/S_j>0$.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform upper product bound]\label{hier:lem:upper}
Every maximizer satisfies $s_1<1-\epsilon_H$, where
$\epsilon_H=(2\log2-1)/(2H(\log H)^2)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
This is the upper bound in Theorem~\ref{geom:thm:global}, applied with
no prescribed equalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Canonical thresholds]\label{hier:lem:alpha}
For real $h>1$ define
\[
 \alpha_h=\frac{\log((h-1)/\log h)}{\log h}
 =1-\frac{\log(h\log h/(h-1))}{\log h}.
\]
Then $\alpha_h>1/2$ and $\alpha_h$ is strictly increasing.
In particular, $2^{\alpha_2}\log2=1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $y=\log h$ and $z=y/2$. Direct calculation gives
\[
 \alpha_h=\frac12+\frac{\log(\sinh z/z)}{2z}.
\]
The second term is positive. Its derivative has the sign of
\[
 N(z)=z\coth z-1-\log(\sinh z/z).
\]
Here $N(0+)=0$ and $N'(z)=1/z-z/\sinh^2z>0$. This proves both
assertions without a discrete approximation.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Transported natural intensities]\label{hier:lem:transport}
For $i<j$ at positive products,
\begin{equation}
 Z_i\prod_{q=i}^{j-1}\beta_q
 =Z_j\prod_{q=i}^{j-1}\beta_q^{\,1-s_q}\le Z_j.
 \label{hier:eq:transport}
\end{equation}
If $s_1<1$, the inequality is strict.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The one-edge identity $Z_q\beta_q=Z_{q+1}\beta_q^{1-s_q}$ follows
directly from \eqref{hier:eq:G}--\eqref{hier:eq:node}. Multiplication telescopes.
Since $0<\beta_q<1$, the conclusions follow.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Global product compactness]\label{hier:thm:compact}
For $H\ge3$ and every positive length vector, every maximizer satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \alpha_2<s_m\le s_1<1-\epsilon_H. \label{hier:eq:compact}
\end{equation}
For the exceptional one-node chain $H=2$, the unique maximizing
product is $\alpha_2$. In particular all products, local ratios and
finite positive mark probabilities used below lie in compact sets
determined by $H$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{hier:lem:upper} already gives the upper bound. Let $a,\ldots,m$
be the bottom maximal plateau, with product $\sigma\le\alpha_2$.
Raising its common product is feasible. Put
\[
 I_{\rm in}=\sum_{i<a}L_iZ_i\prod_{q=i}^{a-1}\beta_q.
\]
The derivative in that direction is
\begin{equation}
 (h_a-1)V_{a-1}-I_{\rm in}\log h_a
 +\sum_{i\ge a}L_i\bigl(h_i-1-h_i^\sigma\log h_i\bigr).
 \label{hier:eq:bottomderiv}
\end{equation}
The derivative remains valid from the right at $\sigma=0$, since
all older products are positive and the bottom recursion is
$G_i=\sigma\log h_i$. Transport bounds the incoming term by
$I_{\rm in}\le h_a^\sigma V_{a-1}$. Lemma~\ref{hier:lem:alpha}
then makes every bracket in \eqref{hier:eq:bottomderiv} nonnegative,
and every bracket with $h_i>2$ positive. Any such rank in the
bottom plateau therefore makes \eqref{hier:eq:bottomderiv} strictly
positive along a feasible variation. Otherwise the plateau is the single rank
$h_m=2$, with $a=m>1$ when $H\ge3$. In that case
$I_{\rm in}<2^\sigma V_{m-1}$ by Lemma~\ref{hier:lem:upper} and the
strict transport identity, so the derivative is again positive,
even at $\sigma=\alpha_2$. Both alternatives contradict maximality.
For the chain $H=2$, directly differentiating
$L(1+s-2^s)$ gives its unique maximizer $\alpha_2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact node margins and root centering}

The first derivatives have two different uses. Their individual
stationarity equations record the reserve at each order constraint;
their weighted sum centers the one uncolored root condition. The latter
identity is exact because the recursive logarithms are homogeneous,
including on a face where several products coincide.

We now work at a maximizer. The preceding result removes the upper
and lower faces of the ordered simplex. There are multipliers
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_0=\lambda_m=0,\quad \lambda_j\ge0,\quad
 \partial_jJ=\lambda_{j-1}-\lambda_j,\quad
 \lambda_j(s_j-s_{j+1})=0\quad(j<m).
 \label{hier:eq:KKT}
\end{equation}
Write $m_j=\lambda_j-\lambda_{j-1}$. A maximal plateau is a
maximal interval $[a,b]$ on which the products are equal. Its exterior
multipliers satisfy $\lambda_{a-1}=\lambda_b=0$.

\begin{lemma}[Node equations and Euler root identity]\label{hier:lem:KKT}
For every $j$,
\begin{equation}
 A_j\sum_{i\le j}L_iZ_i\prod_{q=i}^{j-1}\beta_q=p_jV_j+m_j.
 \label{hier:eq:nodebalance}
\end{equation}
Let $r_j=s_j/s_1$, $a_j=\log S_j$ and
$\mu_j=L_jZ_j$. Then
\begin{equation}
 T_1:=\sum_jr_jp_jV_j=\sum_j c_j\mu_j,
 \qquad c_j=r_ja_j. \label{hier:eq:rootcenter}
\end{equation}
Moreover $0<c_-(H)\le c_j,Z_j\le c_+(H)<\infty$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Differentiation of the recursion gives
$\partial G_j/\partial s_j=A_j$ and
$\partial G_i/\partial G_j=\prod_{q=i}^{j-1}\beta_q$ for $i<j$.
Substitution into $\partial_jJ$ and \eqref{hier:eq:KKT} proves
\eqref{hier:eq:nodebalance}.
Every $G_i$ is homogeneous of degree one in the products.
Consequently
\[
 \sum_js_j\partial_jJ=\sum_js_jp_jV_j-\sum_iL_iZ_iG_i.
\]
The left side is zero because
$\sum_js_jm_j=\sum_{j<m}\lambda_j(s_j-s_{j+1})=0$.
Division by $s_1$ proves \eqref{hier:eq:rootcenter}. Finally
$2\le S_j\le H$ and \eqref{hier:eq:compact} bound $r_j$ above and below,
which gives the stated constants.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Poisson entropy at the saddle]\label{fp:prop:poisson}
For positive original lengths, let $s=s(L)$ be the ordered optimizer
in \eqref{profile:saddle}. With $\mathcal Q(z)=z\log z-z+1$,
\begin{equation}\label{fp:eq:poisson}
 J(L;s)=\sum_{i=1}^k L_i\mathcal Q(Z_i).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $J$ is the relative entropy of independent Poisson counts
with means $L_iZ_i$ with respect to independent counts with means $L_i$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The upper and lower simplex faces are inactive, so dilation of all
products is feasible in both directions, even on an equality face.
Homogeneity of the $G_i$ and stationarity give
\[
 0=\sum_j s_j\partial_{s_j}J
   =\sum_j s_jV_j-\sum_iL_iZ_iG_i.
\]
Substitute $G_i=\log Z_i$ into \eqref{profile:saddle}.
For a single count,
$\KL(\Pois(Lz)\Vert\Pois(L))=L\mathcal Q(z)$;
relative entropy adds over independent coordinates.
\end{proof}
This entropy supplies the exponential factor of the profile.
The persistence factors account for the additional restrictions on
the conditional bridges.

\subsection{Complete unit-step chains: sign and effective time}

For the divisor problem the alphabet loses one name at each step.
This additional structure makes the local drift nonnegative and identifies
where a long persistence constraint can occur. Away from the first node
of a plateau the drift has a fixed positive lower bound. At the first
node it can be small, and its scale is determined by the incoming length
and the stationarity multiplier. The secant estimate below is what
propagates the first-node sign through a plateau.

In this section only, assume
\[
 H\ge3,\qquad m=H-1,\qquad h_j=H-j+1,
 \qquad p_j=1\quad(1\le j\le m).
\]
The \emph{natural local node drift} is
\begin{equation}
 e_j=Z_jA_j-1. \label{hier:eq:nodedrift}
\end{equation}
The rank here is one. It must not be replaced by the larger rank of
an entire equal-product plateau with its child left unsplit.

\begin{lemma}[A secant threshold with one valley]\label{hier:lem:valley}
For $x\ge2$ put
\[
 D(x)=x\log x-(x-1)\log(x-1),\qquad
 t(x)=1-\frac{\log D(x)}{\log x}.
\]
For $2\le x\le y$,
\begin{equation}
 t(x)\le\max\{\alpha_2,t(y)\}, \label{hier:eq:valley}
\end{equation}
strictly when $2<x<y$. More quantitatively, if $y\le H$,
$x\ge2+\eta$ and $y\ge x+\eta$, then
\begin{equation}
 \max\{\alpha_2,t(y)\}-t(x)\ge
 \Delta_H(\eta):=
 \frac{\eta^2\log(2\log2)}{2H^2(1+\log H)(\log H)^2}.
 \label{hier:eq:valleygap}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $l(x)=\log(x/(x-1))$. Direct differentiation yields
\begin{align}
 t'(x)&=\frac{F(x)}{xD(x)(\log x)^2},\\
 F(x)&=D(x)\log D(x)-x\log x\,l(x),\\
 F'(x)&=l(x)\log D(x)
       +\log x\bigl(1/(x-1)-l(x)\bigr)>0.
 \label{hier:eq:Fprime}
\end{align}
Here $D(x)\ge2\log2>1$, and $\log(1+u)<u$ proves the second
term positive. Thus $t$ first decreases and then increases, allowing
either monotone case, with no flat interval. Its maximum on $[2,y]$
is attained at an endpoint and $t(2)=\alpha_2$. This proves
\eqref{hier:eq:valley} and its strict form.

For the quantitative assertion, throughout $[2,H]$,
\[
 F'(v)\ge\frac{\log(2\log2)}H,
 \qquad vD(v)(\log v)^2\le H(1+\log H)(\log H)^2.
\]
The latter bound follows from
$D(v)=\int_{v-1}^v(1+\log w)\,dw\le1+\log H$.
If $F(x)\ge0$, integrate $t'$ over $[x,x+\eta]$, using the
linear lower bound for $F(v)$ based at $x$, and then use monotonicity
up to $y$. If $F(x)\le0$, integrate backwards over $[x-\eta,x]$;
$F$ is nonpositive on $[2,x]$, so $t(2)\ge t(x-\eta)$.
Both integrations give exactly \eqref{hier:eq:valleygap}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegative local node drift]\label{hier:thm:positive}
On the complete unit-step chain, every positive length vector has
\begin{equation}
 e_j\ge0\quad(1\le j\le m),\qquad e_m>0.
 \label{hier:eq:allpositive}
\end{equation}
If $a$ is the first index of a maximal plateau, then $e_a>0$ when
$a>1$. In addition, for every nonterminal index that is not first
in its plateau,
\begin{equation}
 e_j\ge c_H:=2^{\Delta_H(\sqrt2-1)}-1>0.
 \label{hier:eq:uniformpositive}
\end{equation}
There is no assumed lower bound on length ratios, gaps between
plateau products, or nonzero multipliers.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $[a,b]$ be a maximal plateau with product $\sigma$. At its
first node $m_a=\lambda_a\ge0$. With
$I_{\rm in}=\sum_{i<a}L_iZ_i\prod_{q=i}^{a-1}\beta_q$, the exact
node equation and transport give
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_a=A_a(L_aZ_a+I_{\rm in})-V_a
 \le (Z_aA_a-1)V_a=e_aV_a. \label{hier:eq:firstsign}
\end{equation}
This proves $e_a\ge0$. If $a>1$, strict transport makes the
inequality strict, so $e_a>0$.

For $b<m$ put $C=h_{b+1}$ and $z=\exp(G_{b+1}/\sigma)$;
for $b=m$ put $C=z=1$. Within the plateau
$S_i=h_i-C+z$ decreases by one at each step. At every node its
immediate child weight is $S_i-1$, including the last node of the
plateau. Therefore
\begin{equation}
 A_i=D(S_i)/S_i,\qquad
 e_i=S_i^{\sigma-1}D(S_i)-1
     =\exp\bigl((\sigma-t(S_i))\log S_i\bigr)-1.
 \label{hier:eq:nativesecant}
\end{equation}
The first-node sign gives $\sigma\ge t(S_a)$; global compactness
gives $\sigma>\alpha_2$. Lemma~\ref{hier:lem:valley} propagates
$\sigma\ge t(S_i)$ through the plateau. At the terminal node,
$e_m=2^{s_m}\log2-1>0$.

For $i>a$ with $i<m$, we have $S_a\ge S_i+1$. If $b=m$, then
$S_i=h_i\ge3$. Otherwise $u_b=s_{b+1}/\sigma>1/2$ and
$S_{b+1}\ge2$, whence $z>\sqrt2$ and $S_i\ge1+z>1+\sqrt2$.
Thus $S_i\ge2+(\sqrt2-1)$ in both cases. Apply
\eqref{hier:eq:valleygap} with $\eta=\sqrt2-1$ and then
\eqref{hier:eq:nativesecant}, using $S_i\ge2$, to obtain
\eqref{hier:eq:uniformpositive}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact first-node drift scale]\label{hier:thm:effectivetime}
For the first index $a$ of any maximal plateau on the complete
chain,
\begin{equation}
 e_a\asympH\frac{\lambda_a+V_{a-1}}{V_a}.
 \label{hier:eq:driftscale}
\end{equation}
For $a=1$ this is the exact equality $e_1=\lambda_1/L_1$.
When $a>1$, set
\[
 q_-=H^{-H},\qquad q_+=(1-1/H)^{\epsilon_H}<1.
\]
Then \eqref{hier:eq:driftscale} holds with explicit lower and upper
comparison constants $1-q_+$ and $q_-^{-1}$.
Consequently, with the infinite-quotient convention,
\begin{equation}
 1+\min\{L_a,e_a^{-2}\}
 \asympH
 1+\min\left\{L_a,
       \left(\frac{V_a}{\lambda_a+V_{a-1}}\right)^2\right\}.
 \label{hier:eq:efftime}
\end{equation}
For a non-first, nonterminal node, the left effective time is at
most $1+c_H^{-2}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On the unit-step chain $1/H\le\beta_q\le1-1/H$. Also
$\epsilon_H<1-s_q<1$. Formula \eqref{hier:eq:transport} implies, when
$a>1$,
\[
 q_-V_{a-1}\le I_{\rm in}/Z_a\le q_+V_{a-1}.
\]
There are fewer than $H$ factors in each transported term; the
upper bound uses at least one factor. Write
$w=I_{\rm in}/(Z_aV_{a-1})\in[q_-,q_+]$. The exact equality in
\eqref{hier:eq:firstsign}, before using transport, is
\begin{align}
 \lambda_a&=e_a(L_a+wV_{a-1})-(1-w)V_{a-1},\\
 e_a&=\frac{\lambda_a+(1-w)V_{a-1}}{L_a+wV_{a-1}}.
 \label{hier:eq:exactfirst}
\end{align}
Its numerator lies between
$(1-q_+)(\lambda_a+V_{a-1})$ and $\lambda_a+V_{a-1}$;
its denominator lies between $q_-V_a$ and $V_a$. This proves the
stated comparison. At $a=1$ there is no incoming intensity and
\eqref{hier:eq:nodebalance} gives the exact equality directly.
Taking inverse squares and truncating by $L_a$ preserves comparison
by fixed constants, including the zero-drift case. The final assertion
follows from \eqref{hier:eq:uniformpositive}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The effective time in \eqref{hier:eq:efftime} governs the one-end
persistence scale. The reverse reserve, terminal band, and incoming
private state are treated by the conditional bridge estimates below;
their dependence must be retained when combining local constructions.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A hierarchy of plateau lengths}

A root count requires a block with a substantial fraction of the total
length. Such a block need not be the final original block. We obtain it
by varying a whole plateau: its total drift balances the incoming
budget, and an entropy surplus keeps that incoming budget from being
absorbed at zero cost. This argument works for a sparse chain and
remains uniform as a strict product gap tends to zero.

We return to an arbitrary sparse chain $H=h_1>\cdots>h_m\ge2$.
No sign assertion for its individual local node drifts is needed.
For a maximal equal-product plateau $[a,b]$, let its common product
be $\sigma$. Define
\begin{align}
 (C,z)&=(h_{b+1},S_{b+1}^{u_b}) &&(b<m),\\
 (C,z)&=(1,1) &&(b=m),\\
 n_i&=h_i-C\quad(a\le i\le b),& n&=n_a,& S&=S_a=n+z,\\
 A_*&=E_n(z)/S,&
 \mathfrak e_i&=(n_i+z)^{\sigma-1}E_{n_i}(z)-n_i.
 \label{hier:eq:platformparameters}
\end{align}
The symbol $\mathfrak e_i$ is a \emph{whole-plateau} drift: it
uses the entire exterior rank $n_i$, with the child intact. It is
different from $e_i$ in \eqref{hier:eq:nodedrift}.

\begin{lemma}[Exact plateau balance]\label{hier:lem:platformbalance}
With $I_{\rm in}=\sum_{i<a}L_iZ_i\prod_{q=i}^{a-1}\beta_q$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{i=a}^bL_i\mathfrak e_i
       =nV_{a-1}-A_*I_{\rm in}. \label{hier:eq:platformbalance}
\end{equation}
If $a>1$, then
\begin{equation}
 I_{\rm in}
 =\frac{\beta_{a-1}}{A_{a-1}}
