    \bigl(p_{a-1}V_{a-1}-\lambda_{a-2}\bigr)
 \le\frac{\beta_{a-1}p_{a-1}}{A_{a-1}}V_{a-1}.
 \label{hier:eq:incoming}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The sum of budget derivatives over $[a,b]$ is
$nV_{a-1}+\sum_{i=a}^bn_iL_i$. On the plateau,
$G_i=\sigma\log(n_i+z)$ and its derivative is
$E_{n_i}(z)/(n_i+z)$, including the variation in $z$. The derivative
for an older block is $A_*\prod_{q=i}^{a-1}\beta_q$.
The sum of the KKT derivatives on the plateau is
$\lambda_{a-1}-\lambda_b=0$. Substituting these derivatives proves
\eqref{hier:eq:platformbalance}.

To bound the incoming intensity, use the node $a-1$ immediately
before the plateau. Its margin is
$m_{a-1}=\lambda_{a-1}-\lambda_{a-2}=-\lambda_{a-2}\le0$.
Multiplying \eqref{hier:eq:nodebalance} at that node by the routing
factor $\beta_{a-1}$ gives \eqref{hier:eq:incoming}, with all older
intensities still included in their actual mixture.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Whole-plateau entropy surplus]\label{hier:lem:surplus}
If $a>1$, then
\begin{equation}
 n-A_*\frac{\beta_{a-1}p_{a-1}}{A_{a-1}}
 \ge\frac{np_{a-1}}{2H^2(1+\log H)^2}>0.
 \label{hier:eq:surplus}
\end{equation}
This estimate is independent of the size of the strict product gap
before the plateau.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For real $r>0$ and $x\ge1$ let $D(r,x)=E_r(x)/r$. Integrating
$1+\log(x+t)$ gives
\begin{align}
 D(r,x)&=1+\log x+\frac1r\int_0^r\log(1+t/x)\,dt,\\
 1+\log x+\frac{r}{2(x+r)}&\le D(r,x)\le1+\log(x+r).
 \label{hier:eq:Dincrements}
\end{align}
For the lower bound use
$\log(1+t/x)\ge t/(x+t)\ge t/(x+r)$.
Write $p=p_{a-1}$, $u=u_{a-1}$ and $w=S^u$. Then
$1\le w\le S$, $p+w\le H$, and
\[
 \frac{\beta_{a-1}p}{A_{a-1}}=\frac{w}{D(p,w)},
 \qquad \frac n{A_*}=\frac S{D(n,z)}\ge\frac S{1+\log S}.
\]
Since $x/(1+\log x)$ is nondecreasing for $x\ge1$,
\begin{align}
 \frac n{A_*}-\frac{\beta_{a-1}p}{A_{a-1}}
 &\ge\frac w{1+\log w}-\frac w{D(p,w)}\notag\\
 &=\frac{w\,[D(p,w)-(1+\log w)]}
          {(1+\log w)D(p,w)}
 \ge\frac p{2H(1+\log H)^2}. \label{hier:eq:surplusstep}
\end{align}
Finally \eqref{hier:eq:Dincrements} implies $E_n(z)\ge n$, so
$A_*\ge n/H$. Multiplication of \eqref{hier:eq:surplusstep} by $A_*$
proves \eqref{hier:eq:surplus}. Strict separation of the products was used
only for the zero exterior multiplier, not to obtain its numerical
constant.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Maximal-plateau length hierarchy]\label{hier:thm:hierarchy}
At every global ordered KKT maximizer on an arbitrary sparse chain,
each maximal plateau $[a,b]$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 V_{a-1}\le C_H\sum_{i=a}^bL_i,
 \qquad C_H=2H^3(1+\log H)^3.
 \label{hier:eq:hierarchy}
\end{equation}
For $a>1$, its signed incoming whole-plateau drift satisfies
\begin{equation}
 A_*I_{\rm in}-nV_{a-1}
 \le-\frac{np_{a-1}}{2H^2(1+\log H)^2}\,V_{a-1}.
 \label{hier:eq:incominggap}
\end{equation}
The estimates require no positive length-ratio or product-gap bound.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Combining \eqref{hier:eq:incoming} and \eqref{hier:eq:surplus} gives
\eqref{hier:eq:incominggap}, and then \eqref{hier:eq:platformbalance} gives
\[
 \sum_{i=a}^bL_i\mathfrak e_i
 \ge\frac{np_{a-1}}{2H^2(1+\log H)^2}V_{a-1}.
\]
For every summand, $1\le n_i+z\le H$, $0<\sigma<1$ and
\eqref{hier:eq:Dincrements} give
$|\mathfrak e_i|\le H(1+\log H)$. Hence
\[
 V_{a-1}\le
 \frac{2H^3(1+\log H)^3}{np_{a-1}}\sum_{i=a}^bL_i
 \le C_H\sum_{i=a}^bL_i.
\]
For $a=1$, $V_0=0$, so \eqref{hier:eq:hierarchy} is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A long block in the final plateau]\label{hier:cor:longblock}
Let $[a,m]$ be the final maximal plateau, and select a largest block
$d$ within it. Then
\begin{equation}
 L_d\ge\frac{V_m}{(H-1)(1+C_H)}. \label{hier:eq:longblock}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $W=\sum_{i=a}^mL_i$. Theorem~\ref{hier:thm:hierarchy} gives
$V_m\le(1+C_H)W$. The plateau has at most $H-1$ blocks, so
$L_d\ge W/(H-1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The hierarchy compares the total length of a plateau with its
preceding length. Individual blocks within it may be short. Their
drifts can cancel, and their incoming routing words retain the
dependence needed in the conditional estimates below.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A conditional root count}

The long block just found supplies an unread reservoir. After the outside
data have been fixed in their admitted central windows, exact root
centering places the required reservoir count in a central Poisson
window. Its atom has the usual
inverse square-root mass, pointwise in the outside data. Pointwise
uniformity is essential: the outside path weights may already be very
small, and the root condition must multiply those weights without
changing their scale.

We estimate the conditional mass of a root count in the Poisson model
at the optimizer. The path restrictions will be imposed subsequently.
In block $i$ take an independent homogeneous
Poisson point process of intensity $Z_i$ over length $L_i$, giving
$N_i\sim\Pois(\mu_i)$ with $\mu_i=Z_iL_i$. Any independent private
marks can be attached to these points. Let
\[
 V=V_m,\qquad X_1=\sum_i c_iN_i-T_1,
 \qquad c_i=r_i\log S_i.
\]
The centering $T_1=\sum_ic_i\mu_i$ is exact by
Lemma~\ref{hier:lem:KKT}.

Choose deterministically a block $d$ satisfying $L_d\ge\kappa_H V$
for some fixed $\kappa_H>0$. Either a globally largest block or the
block in Corollary~\ref{hier:cor:longblock} does so. In block $d$, choose
a deterministic subinterval of length $\tau L_d$, where
$0<\tau_0\le\tau\le\tau_1<1$ are fixed. Denote its uncolored count
by $N_R$ and its mean by $\mu_R=\tau\mu_d$.

Let $\mathcal O$ be the \(\sigma\)-field of all points and private marks
\emph{outside} that interval. Then $N_R$ is independent of
$\mathcal O$. Write $N_i^{\rm out}=N_i$ for $i\ne d$ and
$N_d^{\rm out}=N_d-N_R$, with corresponding means
$\mu_i^{\rm out}=\mu_i$ and $\mu_d^{\rm out}=(1-\tau)\mu_d$.
The target $x$ must be measurable in the uncolored part of
$\mathcal O$. Assume, for fixed $A,B<\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 |x|\le A\log(2+V),\qquad
 \mathcal C_B=\bigcap_i
 \{|N_i^{\rm out}-\mu_i^{\rm out}|
                         \le B\sqrt{1+L_i}\}.
 \label{hier:eq:outsidecentral}
\end{equation}
The reservoir and its count have not been read by the target or by
any previously selected outside cost.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform conditional root atom]\label{hier:thm:reservoir}
Define the $\mathcal O$-measurable integer
\begin{equation}
 n_*(\mathcal O)=
 \left\lfloor\frac{T_1+x-\sum_i c_iN_i^{\rm out}}{c_d}\right\rfloor.
 \label{hier:eq:rootinteger}
\end{equation}
For $L_d\ge L_0(H,A,B,\kappa_H,\tau_0,\tau_1)$, on
$\mathcal C_B$ it is nonnegative and
\begin{align}
 |n_*-\mu_R|&\le C\sqrt{L_d},\label{hier:eq:rootcentral}\\
 \Prob(N_R=n_*\mid\mathcal O)&\asymp (1+V)^{-1/2}.
 \label{hier:eq:rootatom}
\end{align}
The constants depend only on the displayed fixed parameters. On
$N_R=n_*$,
\begin{equation}
 x-c_d<X_1\le x. \label{hier:eq:rootinterval}
\end{equation}
For every nonnegative $\mathcal O$-measurable random variable $F$,
including arbitrarily rare outside private-word weights,
\begin{equation}
 \E\bigl[F\ind_{\mathcal C_B}\ind_{\{N_R=n_*\}}\bigr]
 \asymp (1+V)^{-1/2}\E\bigl[F\ind_{\mathcal C_B}\bigr].
 \label{hier:eq:weightedatom}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Subtract $c_d\mu_R$ inside \eqref{hier:eq:rootinteger}. Exact centering
then gives
\[
 n_*-\mu_R=
 \frac{x-\sum_ic_i(N_i^{\rm out}-\mu_i^{\rm out})}{c_d}
 +\varepsilon,\qquad -1<\varepsilon\le0.
\]
There are at most $H-1$ blocks. On $\mathcal C_B$,
\[
 \sum_i\sqrt{1+L_i}\le C_H\sqrt{1+V}
 \le C_{H,\kappa_H}\sqrt{L_d},
 \qquad \log(2+V)\le C_{H,\kappa_H}\sqrt{L_d}
\]
when $L_d\ge1$. Uniform bounds for $c_i$ prove
\eqref{hier:eq:rootcentral}. Since $\mu_R\ge c_H\tau_0L_d$, taking
$L_0$ sufficiently large makes $n_*$ positive.

For completeness, if $n=\mu_R+v$ with $|v|\le C\sqrt{\mu_R}$,
then
\[
 n\log(n/\mu_R)-n+\mu_R=O_C(1),
 \qquad n!\asymp \sqrt n\,(n/e)^n.
\]
Stirling's inequalities now bound the Poisson atom
$e^{-\mu_R}\mu_R^n/n!$ above and below by fixed multiples of
$\mu_R^{-1/2}$. The comparison $\mu_R\asymp L_d\asymp V$
proves \eqref{hier:eq:rootatom} on each admitted outside fiber.
The rounding convention in \eqref{hier:eq:rootinteger} gives
\eqref{hier:eq:rootinterval}. Conditioning on $\mathcal O$ then
multiplies any nonnegative outside weight by this same atom bound,
which is \eqref{hier:eq:weightedatom}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Compatibility with exact margin-carry bands]
Assume $m\ge2$. Suppose, in addition to the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{hier:thm:reservoir}, that a subsequent retained word satisfies the exact recursions
\begin{equation}
 X_{j+1}=(X_j-Y_j)/u_j\quad(j<m)
 \label{hier:eq:rootrecursion}
\end{equation}
and the bands are represented exactly as
\begin{equation}
 Y_j=m_j+y_j+\xi_j-\xi_{j-1}/u_{j-1},\quad j<m,
 \qquad \xi_0=0,
 \label{hier:eq:carrybands}
\end{equation}
where the initial term with $u_0$ is absent. Choose the uncolored
root target $x=\sum_{j<m}r_jy_j$. Then
\begin{equation}
 X_m=\frac{X_1-x}{r_m}-\lambda_{m-1}
                         -\frac{\xi_{m-1}}{u_{m-1}}.
 \label{hier:eq:carrylast}
\end{equation}
The identity is unaffected by which block supplies the root count.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Since $r_{j+1}=r_ju_j$, recursion \eqref{hier:eq:rootrecursion} gives
$r_mX_m=X_1-\sum_{j<m}r_jY_j$. Complementarity in
\eqref{hier:eq:KKT} gives $\sum_{j\le m}r_jm_j=0$ and
$m_m=-\lambda_{m-1}$, hence
$\sum_{j<m}r_jm_j=r_m\lambda_{m-1}$. The carry terms telescope:
\[
 \sum_{j<m}r_j(\xi_j-\xi_{j-1}/u_{j-1})
       =r_{m-1}\xi_{m-1}.
\]
Substitute these equalities and $x=\sum_{j<m}r_jy_j$ to obtain
\eqref{hier:eq:carrylast}. The argument contains no assumption about
the position of the selected reservoir.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Events within the reservoir]
After conditioning on $N_R=n_*$, the reservoir points are uniform
order statistics on the fixed interval and their private marks
retain their original law. A later event $P$ that reads that
reservoir needs a further pointwise conditional estimate at the
prescribed count. For example, if on $\mathcal C_B$,
\[
 c\,G(\mathcal O)\le
 \E[P\mid\mathcal O,N_R=n_*(\mathcal O)]
 \le C\,G(\mathcal O),
\]
then conditioning extends \eqref{hier:eq:weightedatom}, with $P$
on the left and $G$ on the right. The required estimate is pointwise
at the selected count. For the path events used below, these pointwise
estimates are furnished by the bridge theorems.
\end{remark}



\section{Conditional survival and the persistence spectrum}
\label{pr:section}


The binary factors in the structural profile measure how much private
label mass survives a path constraint on a given spatial clock. Their
scale is governed by Gaussian persistence against a random environment.
We begin with that Gaussian problem, establish estimates up to constant
factors, and then transfer them to exponential gaps, exact totals, and
complete cells. The order of integration is common to all these models:
the marks and any permitted count window are integrated conditionally
on the gap or Gaussian environment before the fractional power is taken.

There are two distinct issues in this transfer. Endpoint estimates must
hold under the law already weighted by survival, so that surviving
segments can be joined at constant cost. Approximation failures must
also be small relative to the surviving mass, which may itself tend to
zero. The endpoint filter and the relative coupling estimates address
these issues in turn. The positive-order spectrum and its scalar
deviations describe the Gaussian object beyond the fractional orders
needed for the arithmetic argument.

Write $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb E$ for probability and expectation. Comparison
constants are uniform on the compact parameter sets explicitly specified
below. They may depend on fixed curve amplitudes, endpoint boxes, density
margins, and regularity tolerances. None depends on the length of the
process, its allowed reserve, or a count in the stated central range.

\subsection{The Gaussian exponent and effective finite-time bounds}

The environmental channel is held fixed while the private channel is
tested for survival. Let $X,Y$ be independent stationary standard
Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes with covariance $\mathbb E X_sX_t=e^{-|s-t|/2}$. For $0<\lambda,\rho<1$ put
\begin{align}
 A_t&=\{\sqrt\rho X_s+\sqrt{1-\rho}Y_s\ge0:0\le s\le t\},\notag\\
 q_t(X)&=\mathbb P_Y(A_t\mid X),\qquad
 F_{\lambda,\rho}(t)=\mathbb E_X q_t(X)^\lambda. \label{pr:defF}
\end{align}
We suppress the parameters when they are fixed. The conditional moment
retains fluctuations in the environment that an ordinary survival
probability would average out. The proposition below first identifies
its exponential rate and supplies a finite-time enclosure of that rate.
Finite-grid assertions pass to continuous paths through decreasing
events on nested dense grids and bounded convergence.

\begin{proposition}[Existence and effective bounds]\label{pr:existence}
The limit
\[
 \chi(\lambda,\rho)=\lim_{t\to\infty}-t^{-1}\log F_{\lambda,\rho}(t)
\]
exists. If $b(t)=-\log F(t)$ and
$p_g=(1+e^{-g/2})/(1-e^{-g/2})$, then, for $t,g>0$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{b(t)}{p_g(t+g)}\le\chi(\lambda,\rho)
             \le\frac{b(t)}t,
 \qquad \frac\lambda2\le\chi(\lambda,\rho)\le\frac12.
 \label{pr:effective}
\end{equation}
Thus $g=2\log t$, $t>1$, gives an effective interval of width
$O(\log t/t)$. Finite Gaussian integrals give arbitrarily accurate
bounded values of the endpoints of this interval.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Association gives one product inequality, while separated blocks and
Gaussian H\"older give the reverse inequality with an explicit loss.
Together they determine the limiting rate. We then control the error
in approximating each finite-time moment by a Gaussian grid integral.

The private survival indicators on two adjacent time intervals are
increasing functions of a Gaussian vector with nonnegative covariances.
Gaussian association \cite{Pitt}, in the finite form proved in
Lemma~\ref{pr:association}, first in $Y$ and then in $X$, gives
\begin{equation}
 F(s+t)\ge F(s)F(t).                                      \label{pr:super}
\end{equation}
The function $b$ is nonnegative, locally bounded and subadditive.
Writing $T=nt+r$, $0\le r<t$, proves that its limiting slope exists
and equals $\inf_{t>0}b(t)/t$.

For the separated-block estimate we use the following
finite-dimensional Gaussian H\"older inequality: if a centered Gaussian block vector
has covariance bounded above by $\operatorname{diag}(p_i\Sigma_{ii})$,
then $\mathbb E\prod_i f_i(Z_i)\le\prod_i
(\mathbb E f_i(Z_i)^{p_i})^{1/p_i}$ for nonnegative functions.
This is \cite[Theorem~1(i)]{CDP}. We apply it first to the private
Gaussian blocks and then to the environmental blocks.
Consider $N$ intervals of length $t$, separated by gaps $g$. The OU Markov
property and conditional expectation at their endpoints imply that the
covariance of linear functionals on blocks $i,j$ is bounded in absolute
value by $r^{|i-j|}$ times their standard deviations, where $r=e^{-g/2}$.
Consequently, by $2ab\le a^2+b^2$,
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\Big(\sum_i L_i\Big)
 \le \left(1+2\sum_{k\ge1}r^k\right)\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(L_i)
 =p_g\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(L_i).
\]
This is covariance domination, uniformly in the grids and $N$.
Drop survival in the intervening gaps. Private Gaussian H\"older gives
$q_{\rm joint}\le\prod_i q_i^{1/p_g}$. Applying the same inequality to
the environmental expectation gives
\[
 F(Nt+(N-1)g)\le
 \mathbb E\prod_iq_i^{\lambda/p_g}\le F(t)^{N/p_g}.
\]
The second application acts on the powers produced by the first, so
only one factor $p_g$ remains. Taking $N\to\infty$ proves the first
inequality of \eqref{pr:effective}.

The composite process in \eqref{pr:defF} is itself a standard OU process.
Brownian time change and reflection give its ordinary survival probability
\begin{equation}
 a(t)=\pi^{-1}\arcsin(e^{-t/2}).                            \label{pr:ordinaryOU}
\end{equation}
The inequalities $q^\lambda\ge q$ and Jensen give
$a(t)\le F(t)\le a(t)^\lambda$, proving the range of $\chi$ and also
$b(t)\le t/2+\log\pi$. This last bound makes the width assertion explicit.

It remains to make the finite-time enclosure computable. The grid
approximation has two errors: crossings between grid points and the
positive threshold used to suppress those crossings. At mesh size $\Delta=t/n$, let $G_h$ denote the fractional grid
survival moment with common threshold $h$. Conditional on two composite
endpoints $x,y\ge h$, the intervening crossing probability is
$\exp[-xy/\sinh(\Delta/2)]$. Therefore
\begin{align}
 F(t)&\le G_0,\notag\\
 F(t)&\ge G_h-
       \{n\exp[-h^2/\sinh(\Delta/2)]\}^{\lambda}.            \label{pr:griderror}
\end{align}
Indeed the conditional error probability is first raised to $\lambda$;
Jensen bounds its expectation by its annealed probability to that power.
Write $g_h(X)$ for the conditional private grid probability, so
$G_h=\mathbb E_X g_h(X)^\lambda$. For $h\ge0$ these grid events
are nested for each fixed environment, so concavity and Jensen give
$|G_h-G_0|\le\mathbb E_X(g_0(X)-g_h(X))^\lambda
\le(\mathbb E_X(g_0(X)-g_h(X)))^\lambda$.
The last expectation is the difference of the two composite grid
probabilities, bounded by the total variation under translation;
for $h<0$ reverse the nested events. Translation of the composite Gaussian grid gives
\begin{equation}
 |G_h-G_0|\le
 \left\{\frac{|h|}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
             \sqrt{1+n\tanh(\Delta/4)}\right\}^{\lambda}.
 \label{pr:gridthreshold}
\end{equation}
The squared translation norm is
$h^2\boldsymbol1^T\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol1
=h^2[1+n\tanh(\Delta/4)]$, where
$\Sigma_{ij}=e^{-|i-j|\Delta/2}$. Equal-covariance Gaussian total
variation is at most that norm divided by $\sqrt{2\pi}$.
Taking, for example, $h=\Delta^{1/4}$ makes both errors vanish.
On a bounded cube the Gaussian density is uniformly continuous and the
orthant integrand is bounded and monotone; displaced-threshold upper and
lower cube sums, followed by Gaussian tail bounds, give bounded finite
quadratures. Together with \eqref{pr:griderror} and
\eqref{pr:gridthreshold}, these approximate $F(t)$ to arbitrary accuracy.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Tilted environments and the private endpoint filter}

To join surviving segments, we must control the endpoints under the
measure that their survival moments actually induce. Write
$\nu_{t,\lambda}$ for the environmental probability measure with
density $q_t^\lambda/F(t)$ relative to the OU law. We first compare these
environmental tilts by stochastic order. We then control the private
endpoint conditioned on survival against the fixed environment. This
second estimate supplies the mixed endpoint bound needed at a junction.

\begin{lemma}[Order of the tilted laws]\label{pr:order}
For $0\le\lambda\le1$,
\begin{equation}
 \nu_{t,0}\preceq_{\rm st}\nu_{t,\lambda}
                         \preceq_{\rm st}\nu_{t,1}.          \label{pr:storder}
\end{equation}
For each $a<1/2$,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{t\ge0,\,0\le u\le t}
      \mathbb E_{\nu_{t,\lambda}}e^{aX_u^2}<\infty.          \label{pr:envmoment}
\end{equation}
A nonnegative decreasing environmental path functional has tilted
expectation at most its ordinary expectation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The order comparison follows from association of each intermediate
tilt. The endpoint moment then follows from an explicit description
of the fully annealed tilt.

On a finite grid, the nonpositive off-diagonal entries of the OU
precision matrix make its density multivariate totally positive of
order two (MTP$_2$). Set $Z=-Y$ and
$a_\rho=\sqrt{\rho/(1-\rho)}$. The constraint
$\{z_i\le a_\rho x_i\ \forall i\}$ is closed under coordinatewise
minimum and maximum, so its indicator is MTP$_2$. Multiply by the
MTP$_2$ Gaussian density and marginalize over $Z$. This proves that
$q(x)$ is MTP$_2$. To make this joint integral finite, one may insert
an independent product Gaussian density in $x$; its factors cancel
from the MTP$_2$ inequality after marginalization.

It follows that $\varphi_\Sigma(x)q(x)^\lambda$ is MTP$_2$ and hence
associated. We use here the closure and association properties in
\cite[Proposition~3.4(ii), equation~(3.5) and Section~4.1]{Fallat}.
Under this tilted law, association of an increasing test function
with $q^{1-\lambda}$ gives the right comparison in
\eqref{pr:storder}. Ordinary Gaussian association gives the left
comparison, which also yields the assertion for decreasing functionals.

Under $\nu_{t,1}$ rotate to
$Z=\sqrt\rho X+\sqrt{1-\rho}Y$ and an independent standard OU process
$V$. Only $Z$ is conditioned to be positive. Its density at time $u$ is
\[
 \frac{\varphi(z)\mathbb P_z(\tau_0>u)
                    \mathbb P_z(\tau_0>t-u)}{a(t)}
                 \boldsymbol1_{\{z>0\}},
 \qquad
 \mathbb P_z(\tau_0>v)=2\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt{e^v-1}}\right)-1.
\]
For each side of length at least one the latter probability is at most
$Cz e^{-v/2}$; a shorter side contributes at most one. Separating the
cases with zero, one or two long sides and using \eqref{pr:ordinaryOU}
bounds the density by $C(1+z)^2\varphi(z)$, uniformly in $u,t$.
The rotation gives uniform Gaussian exponential moments for $X_u$ under
$\nu_{t,1}$. Apply \eqref{pr:storder} to the increasing function
$e^{a(x_+)^2}$ and the decreasing function $e^{a(x_-)^2}$ separately.
This proves \eqref{pr:envmoment}; dense grids give the path assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform private filter estimate]\label{pr:filter}
On compact subsets of $0<\lambda,\rho<1$ there exist $a>0$ and $C<\infty$
such that
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E_X\left[e^{aX_t^2}
  \left(\mathbb E_Y[\boldsymbol1_{A_t}e^{aY_t^2}\mid X]\right)^\lambda
             \right]\le C F(t).                            \label{pr:mixed}
\end{equation}
The same assertion holds with simultaneous Gaussian weights at both
initial and terminal endpoints, after decreasing $a$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We control the private endpoint through its mode. Strong log-concavity
controls fluctuations around the mode; contraction of the OU evolution
controls the mode itself by a decreasing functional of the environment.
The stochastic order from Lemma~\ref{pr:order} then bounds that functional
under the survival tilt.

Fix the environmental path and let the private wall be
$Y_s\ge-a_\rho X_s$. The filtered endpoint density has the form
$\mu_v(y)\propto\varphi(y)g_v(y)$, where $g_v$ is increasing and
log-concave. Indeed the conditional OU bridge mean is increasing in its
endpoint, and its constraints are convex; marginal log-concavity is
Pr\'ekopa's marginalization theorem
\cite[Theorem~6, p.~342]{Prekopa1973}, first on a finite grid and then by
a limit.
Thus $\mu_v$ is $1$-strongly log-concave and its mode $m_v$ is nonnegative.
For any such density with mode $m$,
\begin{equation}
 |Z-m|\preceq_{\rm st}|N(0,1)|,
 \qquad |\mathbb E Z-m|\le\sqrt{2/\pi}.                     \label{pr:mode-tail}
\end{equation}
To verify this directly, both functions
$\mu(m+r)e^{r^2/2}$ and $\mu(m-r)e^{r^2/2}$ decrease for $r\ge0$.
Their sum therefore gives likelihood-ratio domination of the radial
half-normal density after normalization.
The density is also dominated in monotone likelihood-ratio order by
$m+|N|$: on $y\ge m$ its ratio to $e^{-(y-m)^2/2}$ decreases, while
on $y<m$ the comparison density is zero. OU transition kernels are TP$_2$;
composition with killing indicators and integration preserve this property.
The likelihood-ratio convention allowing zero densities agrees with
\cite[Theorem~2.1 and Remark~3.6]{DuembgenMoesching2023}; kernel composition
here follows from the MTP$_2$ marginalization just used. Consequently
this order propagates through a killed OU segment.
Raising a wall also increases its normalized endpoint law, by association
under the original truncated MTP$_2$ path measure.

Consider a segment of length $v\in[1,2]$, and set $r=e^{-v/2}$ and
$B=\max(0,\sup_{\rm segment}(-a_\rho X))$. By the propagated
likelihood-ratio order and wall monotonicity, it suffices to use the
larger incoming law $m+|N|$ and constant wall $B$.

If $rm\ge B+2$, an OU-noise tube of radius one has fixed positive
probability and enforces survival. The unconditional endpoint above
$rm$ has a uniform Gaussian tail; dividing by that fixed probability
and integrating bounds the conditional mean by $rm+C$.
If $rm<B+2$, first retain the initial value in
$[e(B+3),e(B+3)+1]$, an event of probability at least
$c e^{-C(B+1)^2}$, and then use the same tube. Dividing the
unconditional endpoint tail by this lower probability gives conditional
mean at most $rm+C(B+1)$. Combining the two cases with
\eqref{pr:mode-tail} yields
\begin{equation}
 m_{\rm new}\le e^{-v/2}m+C(B+1).                            \label{pr:mode-recursion}
\end{equation}
An initial segment of length at most one is handled only once: raise its
wall to its supremum and retain a fixed initial interval above
$e(B+3)$. The same tube and tail argument bounds its mode by $C(B+1)$.
Thus the iteration uses intervals of uniformly positive length; the
single short initial interval contributes only an initial bound.

Partition backwards from the terminal time into intervals $I_j$ of length
at most two. Iterating \eqref{pr:mode-recursion}, including the initial
truncation, gives
\begin{equation}
 m_t(X)\le C\left(1+\sum_{j\ge0}e^{-j/2}
                         \sup_{s\in I_j}(-a_\rho X_s)_+\right)=:\mathcal M_t(X).
 \label{pr:mode-majorant}
\end{equation}
OU suprema on bounded intervals have uniform Gaussian tails. Weighted
Cauchy--Schwarz and Jensen imply
$\sup_t\mathbb E e^{c\mathcal M_t^2}<\infty$ for some $c>0$; independence
of the intervals is not needed. The majorant is decreasing in $X$, so
Lemma~\ref{pr:order} transfers this bound to $\nu_{t,\lambda}$.
Finally, for $a$ small, \eqref{pr:mode-tail} gives
\[
 \mathbb E[e^{aY_t^2}\mid A_t,X]
 \le (1-4a)^{-1/2}e^{2am_t(X)^2}.
\]
Multiply by $q_t^\lambda$, use \eqref{pr:envmoment} and the preceding
mode bound, and apply Cauchy--Schwarz under $\nu_{t,\lambda}$.
This proves \eqref{pr:mixed}. Reversibility treats the other endpoint;
Cauchy--Schwarz first inside the private law and then in the environmental
law treats both endpoints simultaneously. Throughout, the endpoint law
is the private law conditioned on the original survival event.
\end{proof}

The mixed filter estimate turns the rate enclosure into a constant-factor
asymptotic. It also supplies positive endpoint boxes in which two
surviving pieces can be connected.

\begin{theorem}[Constant-factor Gaussian survival]\label{pr:gaussian}
Uniformly on compact subsets of $0<\lambda,\rho<1$,
\begin{equation}
 F(s)F(t)\le F(s+t)\le C F(s)F(t),\qquad
 C^{-1}e^{-\chi t}\le F(t)\le e^{-\chi t}.                  \label{pr:quasimult}
\end{equation}
The second comparison is valid for $t\ge1$. There exist compatible,
sufficiently wide fixed positive endpoint boxes for both Gaussian
channels that can be imposed at a constant cost. These are the boxes
constructed below, or fixed boxes containing them; this assertion does
not prescribe an arbitrary narrow endpoint box.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The Mehler density relative to two independent standard Gaussians is
\[
 k_r(x,y)=\frac1{\sqrt{1-r^2}}
 \exp\left(\frac{2rxy-r^2(x^2+y^2)}{2(1-r^2)}\right)
 \le\frac1{\sqrt{1-r^2}}
       \exp\left(\frac{r(x^2+y^2)}{2(1+r)}\right).
\]
Choose a fixed gap $g$ so large that $r=e^{-g/2}$ makes the exponent
smaller than the coefficient allowed in Lemma~\ref{pr:filter}.
Drop survival across the gap. Apply this density bound inside the private
conditional integral and then to the environmental transition. The two
reference blocks are independent; \eqref{pr:mixed} at their adjacent
endpoints gives $F(s+g+t)\le C F(s)F(t)$. On the other hand,
\eqref{pr:super} gives $F(s+g+t)\ge F(s+t)F(g)$. This proves the first
comparison. Iteration at $nt$ and Proposition~\ref{pr:existence} yield
the second one.

By \eqref{pr:mixed}, excluding any of the four Gaussian endpoints from
$[-R,R]$ costs at most $Ce^{-cR^2}F(t)$ in fractional mass. Choose fixed
$R$ so that their union costs at most $F(t)/2$. Add to each channel
$A(e^{-s/2}+e^{-(t-s)/2})$, with any fixed $A\ge2R$. This preserves
survival and moves all retained endpoints into the fixed positive box
$[A-R,A(1+e^{-1/2})+R]$, uniformly for $t\ge1$.
The Cameron--Martin translation formula \cite{CameronMartin1944}, in
the form including an independent Gaussian initial value given in
\cite[Theorem~2.1]{BarbourRossZheng2024}, applies after the OU-to-Brownian
time change. The density of this shift depends only on those endpoints and is bounded above and below
on the box, uniformly for $t\ge1$. Change variables first in the private
integral and then in the environmental integral. The positive-box event
therefore retains a fixed fraction of $F(t)$. A required fixed positive
lower endpoint level can be accommodated by choosing $A$ first and then
retaining this sufficiently wide box (or a fixed containing box).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Parameter stability}

Exact count conditioning changes the binary proportions and gap means
slightly. The next estimate shows that these changes can be made in
the persistence exponent without losing uniform comparisons later.
Its proof is independent of the size of the time grid.

\begin{proposition}[Local Lipschitz continuity]\label{pr:lipschitz}
On each compact subset of $(0,1)^2$,
\[
 |\chi(\lambda,\rho)-\chi(\lambda',\rho')|
             \le C(|\lambda-\lambda'|+|\rho-\rho'|).
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Whiten a finite Gaussian grid. Its survival indicator is a fixed function
$f$, and $q_\rho=T_s f$, where $T_s$ is the Gaussian noise semigroup and
$e^{-s}=\sqrt\rho$. In any unit direction Gaussian integration by parts
and the one-dimensional rearrangement inequality give
\[
 |\nabla q_\rho|\le\sqrt{\frac\rho{1-\rho}} I(q_\rho),
 \qquad I(v)=\varphi(\Phi^{-1}v).
\]
For clarity, the rearrangement step fixes the value $v=\mathbb E f$ and
maximizes $|\mathbb E[Z_1 f(Z)]|$ over $0\le f\le1$; the maximizer is a
half-space in the first coordinate, with value $I(v)$. Gaussian tail
bounds give $I(v)^2\le Cv^2(1-\log v)$, including both endpoints.
Differentiating under the Gaussian integral and integrating by parts,
\[
 \partial_s\log\mathbb E q_s^\lambda
 =\lambda(1-\lambda)
   \frac{\mathbb E q_s^{\lambda-2}|\nabla q_s|^2}
        {\mathbb E q_s^\lambda}.
\]
Convexity of $K(\lambda)=\log\mathbb E q^\lambda$, with $K(0)=0$, gives
$\mathbb E_{q^\lambda}[-\log q]\le-K(\lambda)/\lambda$.
Since $\mathbb E q^\lambda\ge a(t)\ge\pi^{-1}e^{-t/2}$, both the
$\lambda$ derivative and, on a compact $\rho$ interval, the $\rho$
derivative are bounded in absolute value by $C(t+1)$, independently of
the grid dimension. Smooth approximation justifies the derivatives when
$f$ is an indicator. Integrating these bounds, passing to dense grids,
dividing by $t$, and taking $t\to\infty$ proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The positive persistence spectrum}

The preceding estimates concern fractional orders. Allowing every
positive order reveals the structure of the same conditional survival
cost: higher orders increasingly favor environments with larger private
survival probability. We first extend the constant-factor estimate,
then obtain regularity from a dimension-free curvature inequality.

For the same conditional probability $q_t$ in \eqref{pr:defF}, define,
for every $p>0$ and $0<\rho<1$,
\[
 F_{p,\rho}(t)=\mathbb E q_t^p,\qquad
 b_t(p,\rho)=-\log F_{p,\rho}(t).
\]
Every continuous environmental path is bounded on a compact time
interval. A sufficiently high private OU tube therefore has positive
probability and satisfies its survival constraint. The initial
constraint also gives $q_t\le\Phi(\beta X_0)<1$, where
$\beta=\sqrt{\rho/(1-\rho)}$. Thus $0<q_t<1$ almost surely and
$S_t=-\log q_t$ is finite.

\begin{proposition}[Positive orders and finite-time error]
\label{spec:positive}
The persistence exponent
\[
 \chi(p,\rho)=\lim_{t\to\infty}b_t(p,\rho)/t
\]
exists for every $p>0$ and $0<\rho<1$. If
$p_g=(1+e^{-g/2})/(1-e^{-g/2})$, then
\[
 \frac{b_t(p,\rho)}{p_g(t+g)}\le\chi(p,\rho)
 \le\frac{b_t(p,\rho)}t,
 \qquad
 \frac{\min(p,1)}2\le\chi(p,\rho)\le\frac{\max(p,1)}2.
\]
On every compact subset of $(0,\infty)\times(0,1)$,
\begin{equation}\label{spec:constant}
 b_t(p,\rho)=t\chi(p,\rho)+O(1),\qquad t\ge1.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The association proof of \eqref{pr:super} uses only positivity of the
moment order. It gives $F_{p,\rho}(s+t)\ge
F_{p,\rho}(s)F_{p,\rho}(t)$ for every $p>0$. For $p\le1$,
$a(t)\le F_{p,\rho}(t)\le a(t)^p$; for $p\ge1$,
$a(t)^p\le F_{p,\rho}(t)\le a(t)$, by Jensen and $0\le q_t\le1$.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{spec:linear}
 0\le b_t(p,\rho)\le\max(p,1)[t/2+\log\pi].
\end{equation}
This proves the subadditive limit and its range. The two Gaussian
H\"older applications in Proposition~\ref{pr:existence} likewise apply
to all $p>0$: their private bound is
$q_{\rm joint}\le\prod_iq_i^{1/p_g}$ and the environmental bound is
$\mathbb E\prod_iq_i^{p/p_g}\le F_{p,\rho}(t)^{N/p_g}$.
This proves the effective lower bound without an additional factor
$p_g$.

The remaining task is the endpoint estimate for orders above one.
Integer orders admit a useful representation by several independent
private channels; stochastic order then covers the intervening orders. On a finite OU grid, $q_t$ is increasing
and MTP$_2$; hence the environmental law
$d\nu_{t,p}\propto q_t^p\,d\mathbb P_X$ is associated. If $n$ is an
integer with $n\ge p$, association under $\nu_{t,p}$ applied to an
increasing test function and $q_t^{n-p}$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{spec:order}
 \nu_{t,0}\preceq_{\rm st}\nu_{t,p}
 \preceq_{\rm st}\nu_{t,n}.
\end{equation}
Dense grids pass these inequalities to the path law, including
nonnegative monotone endpoint and short-interval supremum functions
by truncation and monotone convergence.

To control $\nu_{t,n}$, take independent stationary standard OU
processes $U=(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)$ and the cone
\[
 C=\{(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n):y_j+\beta x\ge0\ \text{for all }j\}.
\]
Write $p_C(t)=\mathbb P(U_s\in C\text{ for }0\le s\le t)$.
The environmental marginal under this conditioning is exactly
$\nu_{t,n}$. For $0<a<1/2$, let $v=(1-2a)^{-1}$ and
$f_v(h)=\log(1+(e^h-1)/v)$. Stationarity, the Markov property and
the OU representation
$U_h=e^{-h/2}(U_0+B_{e^h-1})$ give the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{spec:cone-time}
 \mathbb E[e^{a|U_s|^2};\ U_{[0,t]}\subset C]
 =v^{(n+1)/2}p_C(f_v(s)+f_v(t-s)),\qquad 0\le s\le t.
\end{equation}
Indeed the weight changes the variance of $U_s$ from $1$ to $v$;
the past and future are conditionally independent OU branches.
Dividing each branch by $\sqrt v$ and changing Brownian time yields
a standard OU branch of duration $f_v(h)$. The remaining
deterministic multiplier is positive and does not affect cone
membership.

The constraint signals $Y_j+\beta X$ have nonnegative covariances.
Gaussian association therefore gives
$p_C(s+t)\ge p_C(s)p_C(t)$. Since
$0\le h-f_v(h)\le\log v$, the ratio of the survival probabilities
in \eqref{spec:cone-time} is at most $1/p_C(2\log v)$. The positive
orthant is contained in $C$, so
$p_C(2\log v)\ge a(2\log v)^{n+1}>0$. In particular,
\[
 \sup_{t\ge0,\,0\le s\le t}
 \mathbb E_{\nu_{t,n}}e^{aX_s^2}<\infty.
\]
Apply \eqref{spec:order} separately to
$e^{a(X_s^+)^2}$ and $e^{a(X_s^-)^2}$, the latter being decreasing.
We obtain the same endpoint bound under $\nu_{t,p}$. The dominating
integer $n$ can be fixed uniformly on a compact positive order set.

The deterministic private filter proof of Lemma~\ref{pr:filter}
does not use $p<1$: its endpoint mode majorant is a decreasing
environmental functional and hence has, by \eqref{spec:order}, its
ordinary Gaussian exponential bound under every $\nu_{t,p}$.
Combining that bound with the preceding environmental endpoint
bound and Cauchy--Schwarz gives, for sufficiently small $a>0$,
\[
 \mathbb E_X\left[e^{a(X_0^2+X_t^2)}
 \left(\mathbb E_Y[\boldsymbol1_{A_t}
                    e^{a(Y_0^2+Y_t^2)}\mid X]\right)^p\right]
 \le C F_{p,\rho}(t).
\]
All constants are locally uniform. The Mehler gap argument in
Theorem~\ref{pr:gaussian} now gives
$F_{p,\rho}(s+t)\le C F_{p,\rho}(s)F_{p,\rho}(t)$ for all positive
orders. Iterating the two product bounds and taking the limiting
slope proves \eqref{spec:constant}.
\end{proof}

The extension above identifies the exponential rate at every positive
order. To differentiate that rate, we need a variance bound for the
conditional cost under its tilted laws. The next lemma provides this
bound for any convex Gaussian constraint.

\begin{lemma}[Convex Gaussian probability curvature]
\label{fp:lem:curvature}
Let $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ be convex with positive Gaussian measure,
$Z\sim N(0,I_d)$, and
$A(x)=-\log\mathbb P(Z+\beta x\in C)$, where $\beta>0$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{fp:eq:curvature}
 0\preceq D^2A\preceq\beta^2I_d,
 \qquad |\nabla A|^2\le2\beta^2A.
\end{equation}
For $d\nu_p\propto e^{-pA}d\gamma_d$, $p>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{spec:variance}
 \operatorname{Var}_{\nu_p}(A)
 \le2\beta^2\mathbb E_{\nu_p}A.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The Gaussian convolution is positive and smooth. If $U_x$ is
$N(\beta x,I_d)$ conditioned to lie in $C$, differentiation gives
$D^2A=\beta^2(I_d-\operatorname{Cov}(U_x))$.
The Brascamp--Lieb variance inequality
\cite{BrascampLieb1976}, in the form
\cite[equation~(1.3)]{CarlenCorderoLieb2013}, gives
$\operatorname{Cov}(U_x)\preceq I_d$. For completeness, the hard
convex restriction follows by first using smooth convex
approximations to the potential
$|u-\beta x|^2/2+N\operatorname{dist}(u,C)^2$ and then letting
$N\to\infty$. The Hessian is at least $I_d$ before taking the
limit, and Gaussian domination passes means and covariances to the
conditioned law. A convex set of positive Gaussian measure has
nonempty interior and its boundary has Lebesgue measure zero, so
replacing it by its closure does not change these probabilities.
This proves both Hessian bounds. Since $A\ge0$ and its Hessian is
bounded above by $\beta^2I_d$,
\[
 0\le A(x-\beta^{-2}\nabla A(x))
 \le A(x)-|\nabla A(x)|^2/(2\beta^2).
\]
Finally the potential $|x|^2/2+pA(x)$ has Hessian at least $I_d$.
Brascamp--Lieb, followed by this gradient bound, proves
\eqref{spec:variance}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Structure and regularity of the spectrum]
\label{fp:thm:regularity}
For each $0<\rho<1$, the function $p\mapsto\chi(p,\rho)$ extends
continuously to $p=0$ with $\chi(0,\rho)=0$, is concave, and belongs
to $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,\infty))$. It is strictly increasing,
with
\[
 \partial_p\chi(p,\rho)>0,\quad
 \chi(1,\rho)=\tfrac12,\quad
 \lim_{p\to\infty}\chi(p,\rho)=\infty,\quad
 \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\chi(p,\rho)}p
 =\lim_{p\to\infty}\partial_p\chi(p,\rho)=0.
\]
The function $\chi$ is jointly locally Lipschitz in $(p,\rho)$,
and $\partial_p\chi$ is jointly continuous. On compact positive
parameter sets,
\begin{align}
 |\partial_p\chi(p,\rho)-\partial_p\chi(p,\rho')|
 &\le C|\rho-\rho'|^{1/2},\label{spec:rho-holder}\\
 \partial_p b_t(p,\rho)
 &=t\partial_p\chi(p,\rho)+O(\sqrt t),\qquad t\ge1.
 \label{spec:derivative-rate}
\end{align}
For fixed $p<1$, $\chi(p,\rho)$ is nondecreasing in $\rho$; for
fixed $p>1$ it is nonincreasing in $\rho$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The curvature lemma gives uniform control of the first two order
derivatives on finite grids. We pass those bounds to continuous paths
and to the limiting rate, determine the order boundaries, and finally
treat the dependence on the correlation parameter.

For a finite time grid with covariance $\Sigma$, whiten both
Gaussian channels. The survival cone becomes
$C=\Sigma^{-1/2}\mathbb R_+^d$, and the conditional negative log
probability is the $A$ of Lemma~\ref{fp:lem:curvature}.
For $b=-\log\mathbb E e^{-pA}$,
\[
 b'=\mathbb E_{\nu_p}A\ge0,
 \qquad -b''=\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_p}(A)
 \le2\beta^2b'.
\]
Concavity and $b(0)=0$ give $b'(p)\le b(p)/p$.
The annealed grid survival is at least $a(t)$, so
\eqref{spec:linear} also bounds its $b$. Thus for $t\ge1$ the
functions $b_t/t$ have bounded first derivatives and Lipschitz
first derivatives, uniformly on compact positive parameter sets
and independently of the grid dimension.

Refine nested dense grids that include both endpoints. Their
conditional probabilities decrease to $q_t$, and the negative
logarithms increase to $S_t$. On every compact positive $p$ interval,
$x^j e^{-px}$ is bounded uniformly for $j=0,1,2$ and $x\ge0$.
Dominated convergence therefore passes the first two order derivatives
and the variance inequality to continuous paths, with positive
normalizers throughout.

The first derivatives of $b_t/t$ are equicontinuous. Any convergent
subsequence of them can be integrated over a compact order interval;
the pointwise limiting slope then identifies its limit as the
derivative of the same limiting function. Hence the limit is $C^1$,
its derivative is locally Lipschitz, and the derivatives converge
locally uniformly. Concavity and monotonicity pass to the limit as
well.

For a fixed $t>0$, $b_t(p,\rho)\to0$ as $p\downarrow0$, so the
upper effective bound proves $\chi(p,\rho)\to0$.
For fixed $t,g>0$, $q_t<1$ almost surely gives
$b_t(p,\rho)\to\infty$ as $p\to\infty$ by dominated convergence.
The lower effective bound then proves $\chi(p,\rho)\to\infty$.
Concavity and nondecreasingness imply
$\partial_p\chi>0$: a zero derivative at a finite positive order
would force the function to be constant thereafter.
For fixed $t$, the essential supremum of $q_t$ is $1$. Indeed,
the environmental event $\inf_{[0,t]}X_s\ge M$ has positive
probability and on it
$q_t\ge\mathbb P(\inf_{[0,t]}Y_s\ge-\beta M)\to1$ as
$M\to\infty$. Hence $b_t(p,\rho)/p\to0$; explicitly, for each
$\epsilon>0$,
$F_{p,\rho}(t)\ge\mathbb P(S_t\le\epsilon)e^{-p\epsilon}$.
The upper effective bound proves $\chi(p,\rho)/p\to0$.
Concavity gives $0\le\partial_p\chi\le\chi/p$, proving the last
limit. The identity at $p=1$ follows from \eqref{pr:ordinaryOU}.

For dependence on $\rho$, the whitened grid probability is
$q_\rho=T_u\boldsymbol1_C$ with $u=-\tfrac12\log\rho$; the cone
is unchanged because it is invariant under positive scaling.
The semigroup calculation in Proposition~\ref{pr:lipschitz},
with $p$ in place of $\lambda$, gives
\[
 \partial_u\log\mathbb E q_\rho^p
 =p(1-p)\frac{\mathbb E q_\rho^{p-2}|\nabla q_\rho|^2}
                    {\mathbb E q_\rho^p}.
\]
The dimension-free gradient bound and Gaussian tail estimate used
there show that its absolute value is at most
$C(1+\mathbb E_{\nu_p}S_t)$ on compact positive parameter sets.
Since $\mathbb E_{\nu_p}S_t=b_t'(p)\le b_t(p)/p$,
\eqref{spec:linear} bounds this by $C(t+1)$.
All approximation limits can be justified with a slightly smaller
positive order, which dominates the logarithmic factors.
Integration of these parameter bounds proves joint local
Lipschitz continuity after taking limiting slopes. The displayed
sign also proves the stated monotonicity in $\rho$.

By \eqref{spec:constant}, $b_t/t$ approximates $\chi$ with error
$O(t^{-1})$. Comparing derivatives with difference quotients of
length $t^{-1/2}$, using their uniform Lipschitz bounds in $p$,
gives \eqref{spec:derivative-rate}. Finally compare difference
quotients of $\chi$ at $\rho$ and $\rho'$ with a common order
step $|\rho-\rho'|^{1/2}$. Joint Lipschitz continuity of $\chi$
and the uniform Lipschitz bound on its order derivative give
\eqref{spec:rho-holder}, hence joint continuity.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A strict annealing gap}

Jensen bounds the fractional exponent below by the fractional multiple
of the ordinary exponent. The next proposition shows that this bound
is always strict. The mechanism is a separation between the typical
environment and the environment selected by ordinary survival: their
time averages differ by an amount proportional to the horizon.

\begin{proposition}[Strict annealing gap]\label{pr:strict-annealing}\label{fp:thm:annealing}
For $0<p<1$ and $0<\rho<1$,
\[
 \chi(p,\rho)-\frac p2
 \ge \frac{\rho}{16\pi}\min\{p,1-p\}>0.
\]
In particular the gap is uniformly positive on every compact subset
of $(0,1)^2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $\mathsf P_t$ be the law of the environmental path $X$ on $[0,t]$,
and let $\mathsf Q_t$ be its law conditional on $A_t$. Its density is
\[
 f_t=\frac{d\mathsf Q_t}{d\mathsf P_t}=\frac{q_t}{a(t)}.
\]
For $H_t=\int_0^tX_s\,ds$, direct integration of the covariance gives
\[
 v_t=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathsf P_t}H_t
     =4t-8(1-e^{-t/2})\le4t.
\]
Rotate the two independent OU channels to
$Z=\sqrt\rho X+\sqrt{1-\rho}Y$ and an independent standard OU
channel $V$, so that $X=\sqrt\rho Z+\sqrt{1-\rho}V$.
Only $Z$ is conditioned. By stationarity, reversibility and the Markov
property, its density at $s\in[0,t]$ conditional on $A_t$ is proportional
to
\[
 \varphi(z)h_s(z)h_{t-s}(z)\boldsymbol1_{\{z>0\}},
 \qquad h_u(z)=\mathbb P_z(\tau_0>u).
\]
For $u>0$ the Brownian time change gives
$h_u(z)=2\Phi(z/\sqrt{e^u-1})-1$; set $h_0(z)=1$ for $z>0$.
Both factors are increasing in $z$. Weighting a positive half-normal
by their increasing product increases its mean: this follows by
integrating $(z-z')[h_s(z)h_{t-s}(z)-h_s(z')h_{t-s}(z')]\ge0$
against two independent copies of that half-normal law. Hence
\[
 \mathbb E_{\mathsf Q_t}H_t
 \ge \sqrt{2\rho/\pi}\,t=:m_0t.
\]

To turn this separation of means into an exponential separation of
the two laws, we use concentration under the convex survival constraint.
If $G$ is a standard finite-dimensional Gaussian vector, $C$ is a
convex set of positive Gaussian measure, and $L=\ell\cdot G$,
completion of the square gives
\[
 \log\mathbb E[e^{\theta L}\mid G\in C]
 =\frac{\theta^2|\ell|^2}{2}
  +\log\mathbb P(G+\theta\ell\in C)-\log\mathbb P(G\in C).
\]
The translated probability is log-concave in $\theta$ by Pr\'ekopa's
marginalization theorem \cite[Theorem~6, p.~342]{Prekopa1973}.
Its tangent at zero therefore proves
\[
 \mathbb E[e^{\theta(L-\mathbb E[L\mid G\in C])}
                  \mid G\in C]
 \le e^{\theta^2\operatorname{Var}(L)/2},\qquad\theta\in\mathbb R.
\]
Apply this fact to the jointly Gaussian vector comprising $H_t$ and
a finite survival grid; if its covariance is singular, represent it
on its Gaussian linear support before whitening. The grid constraint
is convex. Along nested dense grids its probabilities decrease to
$a(t)>0$. Gaussian integrability passes the means and exponential
moments to the limit. Consequently $H_t$ under $\mathsf Q_t$ is
sub-Gaussian about its mean with variance proxy $v_t$.

Set $B_t=\{H_t\ge m_0t/2\}$. Chernoff's inequality under both laws
then gives, for $t>0$,
\[
 \mathsf P_t(B_t)\le e^{-\rho t/(16\pi)},\qquad
 \mathsf Q_t(B_t^c)\le e^{-\rho t/(16\pi)}.
\]
H\"older's inequality, separately on $B_t$ and its complement, yields
\begin{align*}
 \int f_t^p\,d\mathsf P_t
 &\le \mathsf Q_t(B_t)^p\mathsf P_t(B_t)^{1-p}
      +\mathsf Q_t(B_t^c)^p\mathsf P_t(B_t^c)^{1-p}\\
 &\le 2\exp\left[-\frac{\rho t}{16\pi}
                                  \min\{p,1-p\}\right].
\end{align*}
Since $F_{p,\rho}(t)=a(t)^p\int f_t^p\,d\mathsf P_t$ and
$-\log a(t)=t/2+O(1)$, taking limiting logarithmic slopes proves
the proposition.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
For $0<p<1$, define
$D_p(\mathsf Q_t\Vert\mathsf P_t)
 =(p-1)^{-1}\log\int f_t^p\,d\mathsf P_t$.
The exact identity
\[
 -\log F_{p,\rho}(t)
 =-p\log a(t)+(1-p)D_p(\mathsf Q_t\Vert\mathsf P_t)
\]
expresses the annealing gap as a positive information cost per unit
time for the change in environmental law induced by survival.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Scalar deviations and the quenched exponent}
The structural theory also describes the distribution of the conditional
cost $S_t=-\log q_t$. Appendix~\ref{fp:app:ldp} proves a full
large-deviation principle for $S_t/t$, with a good convex rate
$I_\rho$ that is finite precisely on $(0,\infty)$. Its limiting
cumulant $\Lambda_\rho(\theta)$ is finite precisely for
$\theta<(1-\rho)/\rho$ and is locally $C^{1,1}$ there. In particular,
\[
 \frac{S_t}{t}\longrightarrow\gamma_\rho
 \quad\text{almost surely},\qquad
 \gamma_\rho=\Lambda_\rho'(0)
 =\partial_p\chi(0+,\rho),\qquad
 \frac12+\frac\rho{16\pi}\le\gamma_\rho
 \le\frac1{2(1-\rho)}.
\]
The extended spectrum and the rate function are convex duals, and
positive-order environmental tilts select the scalar value
$\partial_p\chi(p,\rho)$. This gives a probabilistic interpretation of the spectrum: its order
derivative is the conditional cost selected by the corresponding
environmental tilt. The assertions here concern the stationary
OU conditional law. The arithmetic arguments below use the
fractional-order estimates, with their own separately defined accepting
measures.

\subsection{Integrable walls and Brownian reserves}

In the marked walks, an initial reserve, a small drift, and a curved
wall all perturb the flat Gaussian constraint. After Lamperti time
change, these perturbations decay from one or both endpoints. We record
a wall comparison in a form that treats all three through their
Cameron--Martin action and coefficient variation.

For an absolutely continuous shift $h$ on $[0,t]$ whose first
derivative has bounded variation, define
\begin{align*}
 \|h\|_{\mathcal H}^2&=h(0)^2+\int_0^t(h'+h/2)^2\,ds,\\
 J_t(h)&=|h(0)/2-h'(0)|+|h'(t)+h(t)/2|
                         +\bigl\|(h/4)\,ds-dh'\bigr\|_{\mathrm{TV},(0,t)}.
\end{align*}
Endpoint derivatives are one-sided traces. In expressions containing
$h''$, use the distributional derivative of $h'$: the last term
is the total variation of the signed measure $(h/4)\,ds-dh'$ on
$(0,t)$. Thus jumps of the first derivative are included, whereas
jumps of $h$ itself are excluded. The corresponding linear integral
below is a signed-measure integral against the continuous OU path.

\begin{lemma}[Bounded-action walls]\label{pr:wall}
For $b/\sqrt\rho$ in this class, replacing the zero composite OU wall
by a deterministic wall $b$ changes
$F(t)$ by a factor bounded above and below whenever
$J_t(b/\sqrt\rho)+\|b/\sqrt\rho\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ is bounded.
An endpoint-restricted version holds with compatible sufficiently wide
boxes chosen after the wall bound, or with the endpoint boxes supplied
by Theorem~\ref{pr:gaussian} translated together with the path.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The Cameron--Martin linear functional is
\[
 L_h(X)=(h(0)/2-h'(0))X_0+(h'(t)+h(t)/2)X_t
                   +\int_{(0,t)}X_s\bigl((h(s)/4)\,ds-dh'(s)\bigr).
\]
Environmental translation alone gives exactly
$F_b(t)/F(t)=\mathbb E_{\nu_{t,\lambda}}
\exp[-L_h(X)-\|h\|_{\mathcal H}^2/2]$, with $h=b/\sqrt\rho$ and the
consistent translation sign. The absolute variation of the coefficients
of $L_h$ is bounded. Jensen with its normalized absolute coefficient
measure and \eqref{pr:envmoment} bounds both exponential signs uniformly.
Jensen also supplies a positive lower bound, or equivalently use the
bound for $\mathbb E_{\nu}|L_h|$. Mixed endpoint moments, followed by
Cauchy--Schwarz and truncation, give the same conclusion for compatible
sufficiently wide boxes chosen after the fixed wall bound. Equivalently,
translate the endpoint
boxes in the same environmental change of variables. A fixed feasible
interior margin and a finite initial or terminal tube permit the
sufficiently wide compatible central boxes used below; their constants
are chosen after the wall and drift bounds.
The comparison holds at the original power $\lambda$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Brownian one-end estimate]\label{pr:brownian}
Let independent Brownian channels have environmental variance $\sigma_E^2$
and private variance $\sigma_C^2$, bounded above and below by positive
constants. Put $\rho=\sigma_E^2/(\sigma_E^2+\sigma_C^2)$. From reserve
$h\ge1$, over duration $n$, with $|\delta|\sqrt n\le D$, the conditional
private survival probability $Q$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E Q^\lambda\asymp
 B_n(h):=\min\{1,((1+h)/\sqrt n)^{2\chi(\lambda,\rho)}\}.
 \label{pr:Bn}
\end{equation}
The upper bound allows a fixed soft wall $-h-gs^\gamma$, $0<\gamma<1/2$.
For a sufficiently large fixed minimum reserve, the lower bound permits
a strong wall $-h+gs^\gamma$, positive central terminal risk, and
compatible sufficiently wide central terminal boxes of the separate
channels. Choose these boxes after the compact-law, wall, and drift
bounds; their locations and widths are then fixed uniformly in $n,h$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $h^2<n$, scale from time $h^2$ and use Lamperti time $u=\log(s/h^2)$.
Its length is $\log(n/h^2)$. Reserve, power wall and bounded scaled drift
become bounded multiples of
\[
 e^{-u/2},\qquad e^{-(1/2-\gamma)u},\qquad
 e^{-(\log(n/h^2)-u)/2}.
\]
Their $J$ and Hilbert norms are bounded. Drop the initial time interval
for the upper bound and apply Lemma~\ref{pr:wall} and
Theorem~\ref{pr:gaussian}. For the lower bound prepare, on a fixed multiple
of $h^2$, both channels in positive central boxes using a fixed Brownian
tube. Brownian scaling makes its probability and its endpoint transition
density bounds uniform. Thereafter use the endpoint version of those
lemmas. The preparation has fixed cost before the fractional power as
well as after it. A large fixed minimum reserve makes the normalized
strong-wall amplitude as small as required. If $h$ is comparable to or
larger than $\sqrt n$, a fixed-scale positive tube and monotonicity give
a constant lower bound; the upper bound is one. Reflection of both
channels proves the same assertions for the opposite risk sign.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Independent exponential gaps: relative coupling}

We now transfer the Gaussian estimate to a rank walk. The gap sequence
is the environment and the marks form the private channel. A coupling
with small absolute failure probability is insufficient when survival
is rare. We therefore establish preparation and reserve comparisons
first, use them to bound each coupling failure relative to survival,
and only then insert the Gaussian wall estimate.

Let $C_i$ be iid marks in a fixed finite alphabet, with probabilities in
a compact subset of its open simplex. Their weights have two values,
\[
 w(C_i)=l-bB_i\in[w_*,l],\qquad
 p=\mathbb P(B_i=1),\qquad \omega=l-bp,
\]
where all parameters range over compact sets, $b,w_*>0$, and $p$ stays
away from zero and one. Independent gaps $E_i$ have exponential mean
$\tau$ in a positive compact interval. Write
\begin{equation}
 S_j=\sum_{i\le j}(w(C_i)-E_i),\quad
 \delta=\omega-\tau,\quad
 \rho_\tau=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+b^2p(1-p)},\quad
 F_n(h)=\mathbb E\mathbb P_C\{\min_{j\le n}S_j\ge-h\mid E\}^{\lambda}.
 \label{pr:walk}
\end{equation}
The following arguments also apply to $-S$, with all monotonicities
reversed together. Assume initially $|\delta|\sqrt n\le D$.

\begin{lemma}[Preparation and reserve comparisons]
\label{pr:crude}
Uniformly for $h\ge1$, $u\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 F_n(h)\ge c_D n^{-1/2},\qquad
 F_n(h+u)\le C_D(1+u)F_n(h),\qquad
 F_{2n}(h)\ge c_D F_n(h).                                 \label{pr:crudeineq}
\end{equation}
The drift bound for a doubled interval is enlarged by a fixed factor.
The preparation comparison also applies to a negative soft wall
$-g j^\gamma$. Positive walls are treated using flat survival to bound
the exceptional events and the strong Gaussian lower estimate;
see Section~\ref{supp:single-block-source}.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The preparation raises the walk to a prescribed height while keeping
both channel totals central. Optional stopping supplies the entrance
probability, and a positive scaled tube supplies the continuation. For the centered
walk stopped on leaving $[-h_0,B]$, upper overshoots are bounded and lower
overshoots have exponential tails; for the reversed walk these roles
are interchanged. Optional stopping of the walk gives an upper-exit
probability comparable to $1/B$, from a fixed reserve $h_0>0$.
Stopping its square minus the variance times time bounds the mean exit
time by $C B$: on an upper exit its squared displacement is $O(B^2)$
and that exit has probability $O(1/B)$; on a lower exit the second
moment is bounded. Truncation first justifies both stopping identities.
By Markov's inequality, a sufficiently large fixed multiple of $B^2$
retains a fixed fraction of the upper exits. From height $B$, a positive
scaled tube over a further comparable time has probability bounded below
by the functional central limit theorem, uniformly on our compact laws.
It can end above any prescribed fixed multiple of $B$.
The lower-overshoot memoryless law and bounded upper overshoot provide
uniformity at entrance. The stopped centered gap and mark martingales
have second moments at most $C\mathbb E\tau_{\rm exit}\le CB$.
Their probability of exceeding $RB$ before the retained entrance is
therefore at most $C/(R^2B)$. Choosing fixed $R$ large retains a fixed
fraction of the $B^{-1}$ entrance probability with both channel sums
central; the subsequent tube preserves centrality at the final time.
Small drift is handled by changing the exponential
mean on the retained central gap-sum tube: if $m=O(B^2)$ and
$|\delta|\sqrt m=O_D(1)$, its log density ratio is $O_D(1)$ there.
The same proof, or its sign reversal, therefore gives a preparation of
length $O((1+u)^2)$ from fixed reserve to height at least $u$, of
annealed probability at least $c_D/(1+u)$.

For $u\le\sqrt n$, let $p_u$ be its conditional private probability.
Concatenating with an independent $n$-step survival from $h+u$, and
using $\mathbb E p_u^\lambda\ge\mathbb E p_u$, gives
$F_{n+m}(h)\ge c_D(1+u)^{-1}F_n(h+u)$. Time monotonicity gives the
middle inequality. The same preparation and tube give ordinary survival
at least $c_D/\sqrt n$, hence the first inequality. For $u>\sqrt n$
these two inequalities and $F_n(h+u)\le1$ suffice.

For doubling, discard environments whose centered prefix gap sum is
unfavorable by more than $R\sqrt n$. Survival has the opposite
coordinate monotonicity, so product association bounds the discarded
$F_n$-weighted mass by the unweighted probability times $F_n$.
Choose $R$ large enough to retain a fixed fraction.

On each retained environment, impose the favorable private count
tail above $(R+D+c)\sqrt n$, or below its negative threshold in
the reversed orientation. A fixed central subinterval of this tail
gives a positive probability lower bound. The event retained is the
whole one-sided tail, with no upper truncation. Its monotonicity
agrees with survival, so association preserves the same fraction of
the conditional survival probability. Its ending reserve is at least
$c\sqrt n$.

From this height, an independent further $n$ steps survive with
annealed probability bounded below by a constant. If $f$ is the
prefix mark probability and $Z$ is the completed probability at the
future environment, then $0\le Z\le f$ and $\mathbb E Z\ge cf$.
Consequently $\mathbb E Z^\lambda\ge cf^\lambda$, and integration
proves doubling. Section~\ref{supp:explicit-relative-bad-construction}
supplies the finite conventions and explicit constants.

The same preparation works for a negative soft wall: after a prefix
of length $m$, the future condition at $-g j^\gamma$ is stronger than
the required condition at $-g(m+j)^\gamma$. For a positive strong
wall, use the flat bad-event bound and absorb its loss against the
bounded-action Gaussian lower comparison, as shown in
Section~\ref{supp:single-block-source}. All preliminary preparation
constants are fixed before any value of $\chi$ is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Relative cost of a bad block]\label{pr:relativebad}
Generate the environmental and private couplings separately on
independent deterministic blocks. A block's sigma-field includes both
original channels, their coupled Gaussian paths, and every coupling
auxiliary. For the early estimate, let $\mathcal D$ be measurable with
respect to whole blocks contained in the first $b\le n/2$ slots;
the sigma-field of these blocks is independent of all variables used
by the remaining slots. Without coupling auxiliaries, it is enough
that $\mathcal D$ depend on the first $b$ original slots. Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E\mathbb P_C(\text{survival},\mathcal D\mid
                  \text{extended environment})^\lambda
 \le C_D(1+b)^2\mathbb P(\mathcal D)^{\lambda/4}F_n(h).
 \label{pr:earlybad}
\end{equation}
For the late estimate, assume that the whole block sigma-field read by
$\mathcal D$ is independent of the whole block sigma-field used by
survival on the first $\lfloor n/16\rfloor$ slots, including every
auxiliary on both sides. Then its relative cost is at most
$C_D\mathbb P(\mathcal D)^\lambda F_n(h)$. In particular this applies
when every block read by $\mathcal D$ starts after $n/4$. Fixed fractions in these
statements may be changed, with corresponding constants. The same
bounds hold for the Gaussian comparison walk and for both risk signs.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If positive jumps are bounded, discard prefix survival and use the
endpoint bound $S_b\le lb$. Independence of the remainder, Jensen over
the prefix, and Lemma~\ref{pr:crude} give the stronger upper bound
$C(1+b)\mathbb P(\mathcal D)^\lambda F_n(h)$.
For unbounded positive jumps divide positive prefix endpoints into unit
bins $[k,k+1)$. Their probabilities are bounded both by
$\mathbb P(\mathcal D)$ and by
$C\exp[-c\min(k^2/b,k)]$, with the fixed $O_D(\sqrt b)$ drift displacement
absorbed in the constants and a first group of bins. Apply the reserve
comparison bin by bin. Using the geometric mean of the two probability
bounds and summing the Gaussian/exponential tail proves
\eqref{pr:earlybad}; the displayed exponent $\lambda/4$ and quadratic
polynomial are deliberately weaker than necessary. Negative endpoints
can only decrease the available reserve. The Gaussian case has the same
tail estimate. For the late estimate retain only survival on the first
$a=\lfloor n/16\rfloor$ slots. By the stated sigma-field independence,
its fractional moment factors from that of the conditional private
probability of $\mathcal D$. Jensen bounds the latter by
$\mathbb P(\mathcal D)^\lambda$, and finitely many doublings compare
$F_a(h)$ with $F_n(h)$. Bounded $n<32$ uses
$\mathbb E\mathbb P_C(\mathcal D\mid\text{extended environment})^\lambda
\le\mathbb P(\mathcal D)^\lambda$ and the crude lower bound.
If a fixed initial coupling block overlaps both read regions, the
lengths below sixteen times that block are also bounded; the same
argument, with the corresponding fixed comparison constant, treats
them without asserting independence.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Relative control of the initial coupling block]
\label{pr:initial-coupling-block}
Fix the compact laws and the bounded scaled-drift range in
Lemma~\ref{pr:relativebad}, and let the fractional exponent satisfy
$\lambda\in[\lambda_*,1]$, where $\lambda_*>0$ is fixed. Fix an integer
$b\ge1$. Couple the centered
exponential and binary channels separately to their scalar Gaussian
channels on the first $b$ slots, independently of all later blocks.
The environmental coupling is outside the private conditional
probability, and the private coupling is inside it.
For every prescribed $\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $H_b$, depending
only on these fixed data and $\varepsilon$, such that, whenever
$n\ge2b$ and $h\ge H_b$, the following assertion holds for each
marginal survival functional covered by Lemma~\ref{pr:relativebad}.
There is an initial good event $\mathcal G_b$ on which the discrepancy
of the two initial risk paths is at most $H_b/8$, and
\[
 \mathbb E\bigl[
   \mathbb P_{\mathrm{private}}
     (\mathrm{survival},\mathcal G_b^c
           \mid\mathrm{extended\ environment})^{\lambda}\bigr]
       \le \varepsilon F_n(h).
\]
The same $H_b$ works for both risk signs. A prescribed fixed strong or
soft curve on this initial finite interval may also be absorbed in
$H_b/8$ by increasing $H_b$ before lengths vary.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $M_b$ be the maximum of the absolute centered partial sums of
both original channels on the first $b$ slots and of the absolute
Gaussian suprema on the corresponding time interval. Enlarge its
definition by the fixed compact coefficients needed to reconstruct
the risk. A union bound using exponential moments of the gaps,
boundedness of the binary increments, and the Gaussian maximal tail
gives constants $C_b,c_b>0$ such that
\[
 \mathbb P\{M_b>v\}\le C_b e^{-c_b v}
 \qquad(v\ge C_b).
\]
The constants are independent of $n$ and $h$. The deterministic drift
on the first $b$ slots is bounded in terms of the fixed data, because
$n\ge2b$ and the full-horizon scaled drift is bounded.
Choose a fixed compact-data constant $C_0$ so that, on
$\mathcal G_b=\{M_b\le H_b/C_0\}$, the two initial risk paths differ
by at most $H_b/8$; make the same choice large enough to pay the
initial drift. A fixed curve on this finite interval has a finite
maximum, which is paid by the final increase of $H_b$.

The bad event reads only the first $b$ slots and their coupling
auxiliaries. Lemma~\ref{pr:relativebad} therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb E\bigl[
   \mathbb P_{\mathrm{private}}
      (\mathrm{survival},\mathcal G_b^c
           \mid\mathrm{extended\ environment})^{\lambda}\bigr]
 \le C(1+b)^2
       \bigl(C_b e^{-c_bH_b/C_0}\bigr)^{\lambda/4}F_n(h).
\]
After $b$ has been fixed, choose $H_b$ so that its coefficient is at
most $\varepsilon$, uniformly for $\lambda\ge\lambda_*$. This choice
does not depend on a persistence exponent or on the eventual reserve
$h$. Since $h\ge H_b$, a change by $H_b/8$ lies between the reserves
$7h/8$ and $9h/8$. The discrepancy bound is restricted to
$\mathcal G_b$; the complement is paid by its relative tail estimate,
allowing every exponential gap to retain its full support. The finitely many experiments $n<2b$ are outside this
lemma and are handled by their explicitly supported finite cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One-end persistence]\label{pr:one}
For $|\delta|\sqrt n\le D$, $h\ge1$, and either sign of $S$,
\begin{equation}
 F_n(h)\asymp_D
 \min\{1,((1+h)/\sqrt n)^{2\chi(\lambda,\rho_\tau)}\}.
 \label{pr:ONE}
\end{equation}
The upper estimate allows a fixed soft power wall of exponent below
$1/2$. For $h\ge H_0$ the lower estimate may retain a fixed strong curve,
a fixed positive central unreserved endpoint, and central gap, binary,
and full-color endpoints. The central boxes are chosen compatible and
sufficiently wide after the compact laws, wall, $D$, and $D'$ are fixed,
before the coupling accuracy and minimum reserve are chosen.
For this endpoint version take $h\le D'\sqrt n$;
larger reserves are not needed for the endpoint assertion.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The construction is given in Section~\ref{supp:single-block-source}; its
quantitative inputs are proved in
Sections~\ref{supp:explicit-rank-coupling},
\ref{supp:explicit-relative-bad-construction} and
\ref{supp:explicit-ou-construction}. Couple the two channels separately
on independent dyadic blocks. The relative early and late failure
estimates, with their full auxiliary sigma-fields, first give comparison
with flat Gaussian survival. The accumulated good-event error becomes
a bounded-action wall after Lamperti time change.

For a positive strong curve, bound the failed-coupling mass by the flat
survival majorant just established and absorb it against the Gaussian
strong-wall lower bound. For a negative weak wall, use its reserve
comparison in the relative error argument. The resulting path inclusions
give the displayed bounds while retaining regularity and compatible
separate-channel boxes. Below the fixed coupling scale, a favorable
supported gap/mark event supplies the finite convention.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact Gamma conditioning and relative local regularity}

Uniform spatial positions correspond to exponential gaps with a fixed
total. We make this conditioning through one joint density for every
selected set of gaps. For a lower bound, a central prefix is followed
by an exact-total continuation of constant ordinary probability; that
continuation is averaged before the fractional power. The same density
comparison then lets us delete local regularity failures at relative
cost.

Let $T_n=\sum_{i=1}^nE_i$ and condition on $T_n=A>0$, where
$|A-n\tau|\le D\sqrt n$ and $n\ge1$. Write
$0<\tau_-\le\tau\le\tau_+<\infty$ for the fixed gap-mean range.
All such conditioning is by a regular conditional
density. Write $\mathbb E_A$ for the resulting environmental expectation.
The private marks remain independent of the gaps and of one another.

\begin{lemma}[Selected-gap density]\label{pr:gamma}
For a deterministic proper set $I$ of $m<n$ coordinates, the conditional density
relative to independent mean-$\tau$ exponentials is exactly
\begin{equation}
 \frac{f_{n-m}(A-\sum_{i\in I}E_i)}{f_n(A)},\qquad
 f_k(x)=\frac{x^{k-1}e^{-x/\tau}}{\tau^k\Gamma(k)}
                          \boldsymbol1_{\{x>0\}}.          \label{pr:RN}
\end{equation}
There is a fixed threshold
$N_\Gamma=N_\Gamma(D,\tau_-,\tau_+)\ge
\max\{1,(2D/\tau_-)^2\}$ such that the following two upper bounds
hold for $n\ge N_\Gamma$: if $m\le cn$, $c<1$, the ratio is bounded
above uniformly on its whole support; for any proper selected set it
has the weaker upper bound $C_D\sqrt n$.
If $m\le cn$, it is bounded below by a positive constant on
$|\sum_I E_i-m\tau|\le R\sqrt n$ for
$n\ge n_0(c,D,R)\ge N_\Gamma$,
with constants depending on $c,D,R$ and the compact gap-mean range.
This threshold ensures that the displayed central set lies inside
the support of the remaining Gamma density.
In the exact-mean case $A=n\tau$, both upper bounds hold for every
$n\ge1$. The central lower bound still requires its stated threshold.
No uniform upper bound is asserted for a near-central bounded-$n$
window that permits $A\downarrow0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Independence and convolution of Gamma densities give \eqref{pr:RN}.
Stirling's formula, uniformly for $\tau$ in its compact interval, gives
\[
 \sup_x f_k(x)\le C k^{-1/2},\qquad
 f_k(k\tau+z\sqrt k)\asymp_R k^{-1/2}
 \quad(|z|\le R,\ k\ge N(R,\tau_-)).
\]
For $k=1$ the supremum is $1/\tau$ and the same upper bound holds.
For $n\ge N_\Gamma$, enlarge the threshold for the preceding central
estimate with $R=D$; the denominator in \eqref{pr:RN} is then comparable
to $n^{-1/2}$, and $A\ge n\tau/2$.
If $A=n\tau$, the explicit density and Stirling's bounds instead give
$f_n(n\tau)\asymp n^{-1/2}$ for every $n\ge1$, uniformly in $\tau$.
The asserted bounds follow; on the central selected set the remaining
total has displacement $O(\sqrt n)$ from a mean with shape comparable
to $n$. The comparison applies to the joint law of all selected coordinates.
Independence is used only in the reference law before exact conditioning.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[One-end exact-total bridge]\label{pr:gamma-one}
For fixed $D,D'$, the compact laws, and a fixed curve as below,
there are $N_{\rm one},H_0$
such that the following holds for $n\ge N_{\rm one}$.
Suppose $|\omega-\tau|\sqrt n\le D$, $|A-n\tau|\le D\sqrt n$, and
$H_0\le h\le D'\sqrt n$. The flat conditional survival probability has
$\lambda$ moment at most $C B_n(h)$, with the exponent of
\eqref{pr:ONE}. A stronger event has moment at least $c B_n(h)$ and can
retain a fixed curve $g\min(j,n-j)^\gamma$, $0<\gamma<1/6$, positive
unreserved terminal risk in $[a_0\sqrt n,a_1\sqrt n]$, and central
full-color windows. The constants and windows can be fixed uniformly
on the displayed parameter range.
One may enlarge $H_0$ after fixing $N_{\rm one}$ so that
$H_0>D'\sqrt{N_{\rm one}}$; the reserve range then itself enforces
the length threshold. The flat upper bound alone also holds for bounded
$n$, by increasing its constant.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All density comparisons below are made after taking
$N_{\rm one}\ge N_\Gamma$ and the required central-support thresholds.
Keeping just the first $\lfloor n/4\rfloor$ survival constraints and
using Lemma~\ref{pr:gamma} proves the upper bound. For the lower bound
first assume $h\le\varepsilon\sqrt n$. On $m=\lfloor n/4\rfloor$
slots retain the strong reference family in Theorem~\ref{pr:one}, with
\begin{equation}
 a_0\sqrt n\le S_m\le a_1\sqrt n,\quad
 |T_m-m\tau|\le R\sqrt n,\quad
 |N_c(m)-\pi_cm|\le R\sqrt n\quad\hbox{for every color }c.
 \label{pr:prefixboxes}
\end{equation}
Its conditional mark probability $f$ has $\mathbb E f^\lambda\ge cB_n(h)$.
The selected-gap density has a positive lower bound on these boxes.
Fix one retained prefix environment and one retained prefix label word.
For $k=n-m$, the remaining exact gap total $A-T_m$ is central. Represent
these gaps as
\[
 E'_i=(A-T_m)\frac{W_i}{W_1+\cdots+W_k},
 \qquad W_i\hbox{ iid exponential of mean one}.
\]
The centered polygonal partial gap sums, divided by $\sqrt k$, converge
to $\tau$ times a Brownian bridge plus their prescribed central linear
drift. Independently, centered color counts converge to multinomial
Brownian motion on the zero-sum hyperplane. Its weight projection has
positive variance. Both convergences are uniform over the central boxes
and compact laws: every parameter sequence has a convergent subsequence;
characteristic-function expansion identifies its Gaussian finite-dimensional
limits, and the uniform fourth-moment bound
$\mathbb E|\sum_{i=1}^k Z_i|^4\le C(k^2+k)$ gives tightness, including
polygonal intervals shorter than $1/k$. Normalizing by $k^{-1}\sum W_i$
preserves convergence by the law of large numbers.

After scaling, the starting risk lies in a fixed positive compact
interval. Choose a continuous path in the zero-sum color hyperplane
whose weight projection stays positive and reaches a fixed positive
final window, and choose the zero centered gap bridge. The multinomial
covariance is nondegenerate on its hyperplane, so a sufficiently small
tube about each chosen pair of paths has positive limiting probability.

A finite collection of these tubes covers all possible retained prefix
endpoints and central remaining drifts. Their probabilities have a
positive minimum; uniform convergence transfers a fixed fraction of
that minimum to the finite bridges. Enlarge the final color windows
once to absorb the prefix deviations. The retained risk is at least
$c\sqrt n$ throughout the continuation and hence exceeds $gn^\gamma$
for large $n$. The first quarter already has the required global curve
from its one-sided strong event. Thus every retained prefix word has
joint remaining-environment-and-mark continuation probability at least
$c>0$.

For each prefix environment let $Z$ be the full successful mark probability
as a function of the remaining environment. Exactly
\begin{equation}
 0\le Z\le f,\qquad \mathbb E_{\rm remainder}Z\ge cf,
 \qquad \mathbb E_{\rm remainder}Z^\lambda\ge cf^\lambda.
 \label{pr:concavecontinue}
\end{equation}
The last inequality follows from $z^\lambda\ge f^{\lambda-1}z$ for
$0\le z\le f$. Integrate against the central lower density in
Lemma~\ref{pr:gamma}. This proves the lower bound. When $h$ is comparable
to $\sqrt n$, a fixed positive tube directly gives a constant lower
bound; alternatively use a smaller fixed multiple of $\sqrt n$ and
monotonicity. The continuation lower bound averages the remaining environment for
each retained prefix word. It retains central full-type windows;
it neither gives a lower bound for every remaining environment nor
assigns constant mass to an individual exact type.
The length threshold also includes the uniform tube-convergence and
endpoint-support thresholds after the windows are fixed. Indeed
$l-\omega=bp$ is bounded below by some $\beta>0$, whereas
$A\le n\omega+2D\sqrt n$. Thus
$nl-A\ge\beta n-2D\sqrt n$, which exceeds $a_1\sqrt n$
for sufficiently large $n$. For the opposite sign the corresponding
available endpoint is $A-n(l-b)\ge b(1-p)n-2D\sqrt n$, and $b(1-p)$
has the same kind of positive compact lower bound. Thus a positive
terminal window is not demanded beyond the possible mark total in
either orientation. The retained central color tubes above
give its actual support. The lower construction therefore uses its stated large-length
threshold, including the endpoint-support thresholds; excluded small
$n$ receive no compactness lower bound. For the flat upper bound in the bounded range, use
$q\le1$ and $B_n(h)\ge n^{-1/2}$ for $h\ge1$.
\end{proof}

Fix a small $\epsilon>0$, $0<\gamma<1/6$, and put $d_n(i)=\min(i,n-i)$.
Let $\mathrm{REG}_K$ consist of the following inequalities for every
$0\le i<j\le n$ and every color $c$:
\begin{align}
 |T_j-T_i-\tau(j-i)|&\le\epsilon(j-i)
               +K[1+d_n(i)^\gamma+d_n(j)^\gamma],\notag\\
 |N_c(i,j)-\pi_c(j-i)|&\le\epsilon(j-i)
               +K[1+d_n(i)^\gamma+d_n(j)^\gamma].           \label{pr:REG}
\end{align}

\begin{lemma}[Relative regularity under the exact total]\label{pr:REGlemma}
Assume $n\ge1$, $A>0$, $|A-n\tau|\le D\sqrt n$,
$|\omega-\tau|\sqrt n\le D$, and $K\ge0$.
If $Q_{\rm bad}(E)$ is the conditional mark probability of flat survival
and $\mathrm{REG}_K^c$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E_A Q_{\rm bad}^\lambda\le C e^{-cK} B_n(h),
 \qquad h\ge1.                                             \label{pr:relativeREG}
\end{equation}
The constants are uniform in the stated near-centered regime.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $0\le K<1$, the flat survival upper bound already gives the
assertion after increasing $C$: for large $n$, retain the first
$\lfloor n/4\rfloor$ slots and apply the selected-gap upper density
bound and Theorem~\ref{pr:one}; bounded $n$ uses $Q_{\rm bad}\le1$.
Thus it suffices to prove the summable interval estimate for $K\ge1$.
Choose a fixed $N_{\rm REG}\ge\max\{32,N_\Gamma,(D/\epsilon)^2\}$,
enlarging it for the fixed-fraction comparisons below, and first take
$n\ge N_{\rm REG}$.
For a single bad interval $(i,j]$, exponential moments and Chernoff give
under the independent reference law
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P(\mathcal D_{i,j})
 \le C\exp\{-c\epsilon^2(j-i)
          -c\epsilon K[1+d_n(i)^\gamma+d_n(j)^\gamma]\}.
 \label{pr:intervaltail}
\end{equation}
This follows by choosing a fixed tilt $z$ with
$\log\mathbb E e^{z(E-\tau)}\le Cz^2$ and $C|z|\le\epsilon/2$;
the finite color variables are even bounded.
We divide the bad intervals according to which short survival prefix
can be retained. This preserves the survival factor in every region
while leaving a proper selected gap set for the density comparison.

For an early interval, $j\le n/4$, retain survival only to $n/2$.
The relaxed event uses at most half the gaps. Lemma~\ref{pr:gamma}
compares its conditional moment with the independent reference moment,
and Lemma~\ref{pr:relativebad} bounds the latter by
$C(1+j)^2\mathbb P(\mathcal D_{i,j})^{\lambda/4}B_n(h)$.

For $i\ge n/8$, retain survival only on the first
$\lfloor n/16\rfloor$ slots. This prefix is disjoint from the bad
interval, and their union omits a fixed fraction of the gaps. One
joint density comparison therefore gives independent reference
variables and the bound
$C\mathbb P(\mathcal D_{i,j})^\lambda B_n(h)$.

Every remaining interval has $i<n/8$, $j>n/4$, and length at least
$n/8$. For a proper gap interval, use the weaker $C\sqrt n$ density
bound in Lemma~\ref{pr:gamma}. For the full gap set, the total is
fixed and satisfies its linear tolerance for large $n$. The gap
conditioning leaves the mark law unchanged. The macroscopic
interval-length tail consequently makes all these errors exponentially
small, including after their $\lambda$ powers.

In the early region, the polynomial in $j$ is summable against
$e^{-cKj^\gamma}$ and the interval-length factor. In the late region
near the terminal end sum in $n-i$; away from both ends the additional
$e^{-cKn^\gamma}$ absorbs the number of intervals. There are at most
$n^2$ macroscopic intervals, and their exponential errors are smaller
