the backward upper tower, so its multiplicative constant does not feed
back into a gate, acceptance probability, bank length, or scalar
cutoff. The positive-core upper holds at every vector with
$\min_i L_i\ge1$. The lower at the explicit lift uses the direct
one-channel theorem in Section~\ref{supp:explicit-ordinary-construction};
its reserve and cutoff, and all collision, history, count, and grid
choices, are independent of $C_H^{\mathrm{os}}$. This establishes the
claimed separation between the explicit profile and the final
comparison constants.

\subsubsection{Harmonic stability, including zero lengths}

For $L_i\ge0$, write $\ell_i=L_i+\log3$ and, for any $\lambda\ge1$,
\[
 L_i^\lambda=\max(L_i,\lambda),\qquad
 \ell_i^\lambda=L_i^\lambda+\log3,\qquad
 \delta_i=L_i^\lambda-L_i\in[0,\lambda].
\]
The unconditional harmonic stability proved in
Section~\ref{supp:dyadic-lift-evaluator} gives
\begin{align}
 e^{-A}K_k(\ell)&\le K_k(\ell^\lambda)\le e^A K_k(\ell),
 \label{threshold:lift-stability}\\
 A&=\sum_{i=1}^k h_i|\delta_i|
 +H\left(\sum_{i=1}^k\left|\sum_{j\le i}\delta_j\right|
                                      +2kC_M\right),
 \qquad h_i=k-i+2.\notag
\end{align}
The harmonic-prime discrepancy estimate permits $C_M=100$.
Since the increments are nonnegative,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i=1}^k\left|\sum_{j\le i}\delta_j\right|
 &=\sum_{j=1}^k(k-j+1)\delta_j
 \le\frac{k(k+1)}2\lambda,\\
 \sum_i h_i\delta_i&\le\frac{k(k+3)}2\lambda.
\end{align*}
Therefore
\begin{equation}
 A\le B_k\lambda+C_0(k),\qquad
 B_k=\frac{k(k^2+3k+4)}2,\qquad C_0(k)=200k(k+1).
 \label{threshold:lift-exponent}
\end{equation}
No positive separation of adjacent cutoffs is assumed. Removing the
primes whose block memberships change leaves one common unnormalized
sum, positive because the empty tuple contributes $(\log2)^k$.
Insertion bounds compare both full sums with that same sum, so the
exponent is not doubled. Equal cutoffs, empty prime blocks, and
$L_1=\cdots=L_k=0$ are included.

At $\lambda=\Lambda_k$, the positive-core upper and the explicit-lift
lower give
\[
 c_k\Psi_k(L^{\Lambda_k})
 \le K_k(\ell^{\Lambda_k})
 \le C_k\Psi_k(L^{\Lambda_k}).
\]
The lower threshold inequalities hold at $\Lambda_k$ and at every
larger original block length; all plateaux and contexts are computed
from the same lifted vector. Combining these bounds with
\eqref{threshold:lift-stability}--\eqref{threshold:lift-exponent} proves
\begin{equation}
 K_k(\ell)\asymp_k\Psi_k(L^{\Lambda_k})=\Phi_k(\ell).
 \label{threshold:fixed-lift-equivalence}
\end{equation}
The factor $\exp\{B_k\Lambda_k+C_0(k)\}$ depends only on $k$.

To return to the divisor count, apply the arithmetic reduction at
the original cutoffs and its original domain
$x\ge2^k(y_1\cdots y_k)y_k$. Substituting
\eqref{threshold:fixed-lift-equivalence} into that reduction proves the
dyadic theorem without imposing a condition on fictitious lifted
cutoffs. The same original-vector harmonic formula enters the
multiplication-table transfer.

\renewcommand{\papertagprefix}{\thesection}
\numberwithin{equation}{section}
\section{Evaluation of the ordered saddle}
\label{supp:ordered-saddle-scalar-elimination}
The profile requires the ordered saddle at every length vector,
including vectors on which plateaux merge. This appendix evaluates
that saddle by eliminating coordinates one at a time. Each elimination
is a monotone scalar equation with endpoint clipping. The gradient
formula retains the contribution of a moving constraint, so the same
recursion applies on every equality face.

We first define the scalar operation and the elementary value and
gradient data. We then state the recursion. A profiling lemma proves
its continuity and monotonicity, and the final reconstruction shows
that it returns the ordered maximum.

\subsection{The scalar operation}

For a continuous strictly decreasing function \(D\) on \([ a , b ]\), define
the clipped scalar inverse

\[
 \mathfrak R(a,b;D)=
 \begin{cases}
 a,&D(a)\le0,\\
 b,&D(b)\ge0,\\
 \text{the unique }z\in(a,b)\text{ with }D(z)=0,
       &D(a)>0>D(b).
 \end{cases}
 \tag{\papertagprefix.1}
\]

For \(a=b\), the interval has only one possible value. On a
nondegenerate interval, the endpoint tests select a boundary value,
or the intermediate value theorem gives the unique interior root.
Bisection evaluates the interior branch to any specified accuracy.
This is the scalar operation used at every stage of the recursion.

The recursion below gives a continuous strictly decreasing function
\(D\) at each step, so the clipped inverse is uniquely defined.

\subsection{Initial elementary data}

The recursion needs both the objective and its gradient. We compute
them on a full positive box so that profiling remains valid before
the remaining coordinates are ordered.

Fix \(k \ge 1\), positive lengths \(L_{i}\), and \(V_{j} = \sum_{i \le j} L_{i}\). Set
\(a = 1 / 4\), \(b = 1\). On the whole box \([ a , b ]^{k}\), not merely its ordered
part, compute

\[
 G_k=s_k\log2,\qquad
 G_i=s_i\log(1+e^{G_{i+1}/s_i}),\qquad Z_i=e^{G_i},
\]

and

\[
 J(\boldsymbol s)=\sum_iL_i+\sum_j s_jV_j-\sum_iL_iZ_i.
 \tag{\papertagprefix.2}
\]

Its gradient has a direct scalar recursion. For \(i < k\) put

\[
 \beta_i=\frac{e^{G_{i+1}/s_i}}{1+e^{G_{i+1}/s_i}},\quad
 A_i=\log(1+e^{G_{i+1}/s_i})
                    -\frac{G_{i+1}}{s_i}\beta_i,
 \qquad A_k=\log2.
\]

Then compute

\[
 T_1=L_1Z_1,\qquad
 T_j=L_jZ_j+\beta_{j-1}T_{j-1},\qquad
 g_{0,j}=V_j-A_jT_j.
 \tag{\papertagprefix.3}
\]

Set \(f_{0} = J\), \(g_{0} = ( g_{0 , 1} , \ldots , g_{0 , k} )\). Equations (2)--(3) are the
initial value/gradient evaluation. They contain \(O ( k )\) arithmetic
steps and no optimization.

The strict concavity needed below follows on the full positive box.
The perspective \(s \log ( 1 + \exp ( u / s ) )\) is convex and increases in \(u\).
Induction makes every \(G_{i}\) convex. In the Hessian of
\(\sum_{i} L_{i} \exp ( G_{i} )\), the contribution

\[
 \sum_iL_i e^{G_i}\nabla G_i\nabla G_i^T
 \tag{\papertagprefix.4}
\]

is positive definite: the Jacobian of the \(G_{i}\) is upper triangular
with diagonal \(A_{i} > 0\). The other Hessian contribution is positive
semidefinite. Thus \(J\) is smooth and strictly concave on this whole
box. Direct differentiation gives
\(\partial_{j} G_{i} = A_{j} \prod_{i \le q < j} \beta_{q}\) for \(i \le j\), which proves (3).

Theorem~\ref{geom:thm:global} implies that the original ordered saddle
satisfies \(s_{k} > 1 / 2\) and \(s_{1} < 1\). Therefore its maximum on the original
ordered simplex is unchanged if restricted to the ordered box
\(1 \ge s_{1} \ge \ldots \ge s_{k} \ge 1 / 4\). This justifies the fixed positive lower endpoint and places every
evaluation away from the zero-product perspective singularities.

\subsection{The finite recursive rule}

At each stage we maximize the first remaining coordinate over the
interval imposed by its successor. We record the maximizing value
and the gradient of the resulting profiled objective. The correction
for the moving lower endpoint is what allows plateau equalities to
be handled by the recursion itself.

For \(j = 1 , \ldots , k - 1\), assume \(f_{j - 1}\) and its gradient \(g_{j - 1}\) are
available as scalar-inverse expressions in \(k - j + 1\) variables on the
full box \([ a , b ]^{k - j + 1}\). For a tail
\(t = ( t_{1} , \ldots , t_{k - j} )\) define

\[
 D_j(z;t)=g_{j-1,1}(z,t),\qquad
 z_j(t)=\mathfrak R(t_1,b;D_j(\cdot;t)).
 \tag{\papertagprefix.5}
\]

Evaluate once more at that root, and set

\[
 f_j(t)=f_{j-1}(z_j(t),t),
\]

\[
 g_{j,r}(t)=g_{j-1,r+1}(z_j(t),t)
            +\mathbf1_{r=1}\min\{0,g_{j-1,1}(z_j(t),t)\},
 \quad1\le r\le k-j.
 \tag{\papertagprefix.6}
\]

The \(\min ( 0 , \ldots )\) term is the contribution of the moving
lower endpoint. It is present when the root clips there with negative
derivative, and vanishes at an interior root or a fixed upper maximum.
For \(t_{1}=b\), formula (6) gives the continuous left derivative of the
profiled value, with the same sign rule.

The last scalar is

\[
 s_k^*=\mathfrak R(a,b;z\mapsto g_{k-1,1}(z)).
 \tag{\papertagprefix.7}
\]

Recover the other coordinates in reverse order:

\[
 s_j^*=z_j(s_{j+1}^*,...,s_k^*),\qquad j=k-1,...,1.
 \tag{\papertagprefix.8}
\]

For \(k = 1\), (7) uses \(g_{0}\) directly and there is no profiling step.
It returns the usual scalar saddle
\(s_{1} = \log ( 1 / \log 2 ) / \log 2\).

For every \(k\), the maximal runs of equalities in (8) give
the plateaux. A lower clipping root can produce a plateau merger. The same branch
handles a zero derivative at that endpoint, so the recursion specifies
the exact equality face without an additional tolerance convention.

\subsection{Monotonicity of the scalar equations}

The recursion is valid because profiling preserves strict concavity
and a continuous gradient. The following lemma also proves that the
moving-boundary correction remains continuous at clipping transitions.

\begin{lemma}[Scalar profiling]\label{scalar:profiling}
Let \(f ( z , u_{1} , \ldots , u_{d} )\) be continuously differentiable and
strictly concave on \([ a , b ]^{d + 1}\), with continuous one-sided
derivatives on its boundary. For each \(u\), define

\[
 z(u)=\mathfrak R(u_1,b;\partial_z f(\cdot,u)),\qquad
 q(u)=f(z(u),u).
\]

Then \(q\) is strictly concave and continuously differentiable on the
full remaining box, with

\[
 \partial_{u_r}q
   =\partial_{u_r}f(z(u),u)
              +\mathbf1_{r=1}\min\{0,\partial_zf(z(u),u)\}.
 \tag{\papertagprefix.9}
\]

The root \(z ( u )\) is continuous. Each derivative
\(\partial_{z} f ( z , u )\) is strictly decreasing in \(z\) on a nondegenerate
interval, so all its scalar inverse branches are unique.
\end{lemma}\begin{proof}
A continuously differentiable strictly concave scalar
function has a strictly decreasing derivative. Otherwise two equal
derivative values and concavity force a linear interval, contrary
to strict concavity. Hence (1) returns its unique maximum on
\([ u_{1} , b ]\). Compactness, continuity of \(f\), and the continuous
endpoints show that a limit of root values maximizes the limit
interval; uniqueness proves continuity of \(z ( u )\).

For distinct \(u , v\), let their two maximizing scalar values be
\(z ( u ) , z ( v )\). At \(w = \theta u + ( 1 - \theta ) v\), the convex combination
\(\theta z ( u ) + ( 1 - \theta ) z ( v )\) is feasible, because it is at least
\(w_{1}\) and at most \(b\). The full input vectors are distinct even
when their scalar roots coincide. Strict concavity of \(f\) gives

\[
 q(w)\ge f(\theta z(u)+(1-\theta)z(v),w)
       >\theta q(u)+(1-\theta)q(v).
\]

Thus \(q\) is strictly concave; the remaining coordinates need not
be ordered for this argument.

For a derivative in \(u_{r}\), \(r > 1\), the feasible interval is fixed;
the elementary envelope inequalities compare the old and new
maximizing values and give \(\partial_{u_{r}} q = \partial_{u_{r}} f\) at the
unique root. For \(u_{1}\), there are three strict cases. At a lower
root with \(\partial_{z} f < 0\), it remains the lower root locally, so
the chain rule adds \(\partial_{z} f\). At an upper root with
\(\partial_{z} f > 0\), that endpoint is fixed and adds nothing. At an
interior root, \(\partial_{z} f = 0\), and the envelope inequalities again
add nothing.

At a clipping transition the derivative is zero, so these formulas
agree. More explicitly, comparing an optimal point with its
projection into a neighboring interval moves it by at most
\(| \,\mathrm{d}u_{1} |\). If the limit optimum is a boundary point with zero
derivative, the resulting value error is \(o ( | \,\mathrm{d}u_{1} | )\) by uniform
continuity of the first derivative. Ordinary parameter changes
are expanded at the convergent optimizing point and give the
displayed derivative. This also proves the formula without
assuming the root itself differentiable. At \(u_{1} = b\), the same
projection comparison from the left yields the extra derivative
when \(\partial_{z} f < 0\), and yields zero extra derivative when it is
positive; this is precisely the \(\min\) in (9). All formulas are
continuous since the root and the derivatives are continuous.
This proves the lemma.
\end{proof}

Apply the lemma successively with \(f = f_{j - 1}\). It proves that
\(g_{j}\) in (6) is its actual gradient and that \(f_{j}\) is \(C^{1}\) and
strictly concave on the entire remaining box. In particular
\(D_{j}\) is continuous and strictly decreasing on every scalar
interval in (5). Thus each scalar inverse used in the recursion has a unique branch.

\subsection{Exact reconstruction of the ordered maximum}

The recursion satisfies

\[
 f_j(s_{j+1},...,s_k)
 =\max_{b\ge s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_j\ge s_{j+1}}
                 J(s_1,...,s_k).
 \tag{\papertagprefix.10}
\]

Induction proves this: \(f_{j - 1}\) has already eliminated the first
\(j - 1\) coordinates; maximizing the next scalar over
\([ s_{j + 1} , b ]\) is exactly the unique root in (5). The value and gradient recursion (3), (5)--(7) therefore evaluates
the ordered maximum using scalar inverses.

The last root (7), followed by the reverse reconstruction (8), returns
the ordered maximum. Strict concavity of \(J\) gives its uniqueness.
The recursion covers all \(2^{k-1}\) possible plateau patterns and
their equality boundaries. The lower endpoint \(1/4\) leaves the
maximum unchanged by the saddle compactness theorem.

\subsection{The finite evaluator and the length threshold}

The depth of the scalar-inverse recursion is \(k\). The initial
elementary computations have fixed dimension \(k\). The stage definitions
are a finite system of \(k\) explicit functions, each using one new
scalar root and the previously constructed value/gradient functions.
Expanding the definitions duplicates at most a number depending on
\(k\) of earlier expressions per stage. For example the crude bound
\([ 100 ( k + 1 )^{3} ]^{k + 1}\) bounds their expression-node count after full
expansion, treating each independently defined scalar inverse as
one operation. This bound is independent
of all lengths. The number of scalar inverse functions depends only on $k$;
the numerical accuracy of each inverse can be increased by bisection.
